CVE-2026-0798.title: Gitea may send release notification emails for private repositori ...
CVE-2026-0798.description: Gitea may send release notification emails for private repositories to users whose access has been revoked. When a repository is changed from public to private, users who previously watched the repository may continue to receive release notifications, potentially disclosing release titles, tags, and content.

CVE-2026-101023.title: Gitea's OAuth2 token endpoint verified the signature and grant of ...
CVE-2026-101023.description: Gitea's OAuth2 token endpoint verified the signature and grant of a token submitted with the `refresh_token` grant type, but not that the token was a refresh token. An unexpired access token for the same OAuth2 application and grant could be exchanged for a new access token and refresh token. Whoever holds such an access token could keep access beyond the token's original lifetime.

CVE-2026-101027.title: When `[migrations] ALLOWED_DOMAINS` was configured, a hostname ma ...
CVE-2026-101027.description: When `[migrations] ALLOWED_DOMAINS` was configured, a hostname matching the allow list was accepted without checking its resolved address against the local-network restrictions. A user who can start repository migrations and control the DNS of an allowed hostname could make it resolve to loopback or private addresses and bypass `ALLOW_LOCALNETWORKS = false`, reaching internal services from the Gitea server. Instances without `ALLOWED_DOMAINS` configured are not affected by this specific bypass.

CVE-2026-101029.title: Gitea's repository migration and pull mirror egress checks could  ...
CVE-2026-101029.description: Gitea's repository migration and pull mirror egress checks could be bypassed with a hostname that returns multiple DNS answers, because the address that was validated was not necessarily the address Git later connected to. A low-privileged user who can create migrations or mirrors could direct the server to internal services, reading from and writing to reachable internal Git or HTTP endpoints. Content from internal responses could additionally be disclosed through migration and mirror error messages.

CVE-2026-103059.title: When Gitea's built-in SSH server is enabled (`START_SSH_SERVER =  ...
CVE-2026-103059.description: When Gitea's built-in SSH server is enabled (`START_SSH_SERVER = true`), the presented public key was looked up with an SQL `LIKE` comparison of its encoded content, which is case-insensitive on some databases, including the default SQLite. An attacker who can construct a case variant of another user's registered RSA public key for which they can derive the private key could have that key matched to the victim's account and authenticate over SSH as that user. Keys are now looked up by fingerprint.

CVE-2026-103504.title: Changing an organization team's permission through the API with o ...
CVE-2026-103504.description: Changing an organization team's permission through the API with only the `permission` field did not rebuild the team's per-unit access, and the requested level was not applied as a cap. After an organization owner demoted a team, for example from admin to read, the team's members kept their previous unit permissions, including write access to the team's repositories. The web form was not affected.

CVE-2026-103667.title: Gitea's container registry served blob downloads with a `Content- ...
CVE-2026-103667.description: Gitea's container registry served blob downloads with a `Content-Type` taken from the media type declared in pushed image manifests, without a `Content-Disposition` or restrictive content security policy. A user who can push container images can publish a blob containing HTML and JavaScript with a `text/html` media type. When a victim who is authenticated to the instance opens the blob URL in a browser, the script runs on the Gitea origin and can perform actions as the victim, such as creating API tokens.

CVE-2026-103670.title: When a Gitea Actions run was inserted, older runs in the same wor ...
CVE-2026-103670.description: When a Gitea Actions run was inserted, older runs in the same workflow-level concurrency group were cancelled without checking whether the new run still needed approval. Because fork pull request runs are inserted under the base repository, a user who can open a pull request from a fork could cancel trusted in-progress runs that share a concurrency group with `cancel-in-progress` enabled, without approval and without running any code. On self-hosted runners this can interrupt deployments and leave partial state behind.

CVE-2026-104626.title: A user who can open a fork pull request can place workflow conten ...
CVE-2026-104626.description: A user who can open a fork pull request can place workflow content with a shared run-level concurrency group into a Gitea Actions run that is awaiting approval. When a later run in that group cancels the blocked job, the run becomes terminal while still marked as needing approval. If a maintainer later approves the run, Gitea passed the already-cancelled job back through concurrency preparation, set it to waiting, and made it claimable by a matching runner, executing fork-controlled workflow code. Exploitation requires the maintainer's later approval action, Actions to be enabled, and a runner that accepts the repository's jobs.

CVE-2026-104627.title: The Gitea OpenID association callback in the security settings ac ...
CVE-2026-104627.description: The Gitea OpenID association callback in the security settings accepted a positive OpenID 2.0 assertion without checking that the signed-in user had started the linking. Because OpenID 2.0 allows unsolicited assertions, an attacker-controlled OpenID provider could attach the attacker's identity to the account of a signed-in victim who opened a crafted link, and the attacker could then sign in as the victim through OpenID login, which does not apply the local TOTP or WebAuthn checks. The callback now requires a time-limited `state` value bound to the user.

CVE-2026-104632.title: Gitea Actions blocks the jobs of workflow runs from first-time fo ...
CVE-2026-104632.description: Gitea Actions blocks the jobs of workflow runs from first-time fork pull request contributors until a maintainer approves the run. The rerun path only required a run to be finished and built the new attempt's jobs without considering the pending approval, so when a user with Actions write access cancelled a run that was awaiting approval and then re-ran it, the new jobs were created as waiting rather than blocked while the run still recorded that approval was required. Cancelling and re-running stale fork checks is a routine action that does not involve the approval control, so where Actions is enabled and a matching runner is registered, workflow code taken from the fork pull request head could run on the repository's runners without an explicit approval.

CVE-2026-104633.title: When migrating a repository from another Gitea instance, Gitea us ...
CVE-2026-104633.description: When migrating a repository from another Gitea instance, Gitea used the page size reported in the source server's API settings to end its paginated downloads. A source that reported `max_response_items` as `0` made these loops run indefinitely and grow server memory until it was exhausted. Any user who can migrate repositories could point a migration at a server they control and cause a denial of service.

CVE-2026-104636.title: Gitea validated the initial remote URL for push mirrors, wiki rem ...
CVE-2026-104636.description: Gitea validated the initial remote URL for push mirrors, wiki remote checks, and fetches of migrated pull request heads, but the subsequent raw Git operations followed HTTP redirects without revalidating the destination. A repository administrator using a policy-allowed endpoint that redirects could make Gitea's Git client send requests to an address that the outbound host policy would otherwise block. The impact depends on the configured policy and the internal services reachable from the server.

CVE-2026-105267.title: The Gitea web route for deleting tags (`POST /{owner}/{repo}/tags ...
CVE-2026-105267.description: The Gitea web route for deleting tags (`POST /{owner}/{repo}/tags/delete`) requires only write access to the Code unit, but shares its handler with release deletion and did not check that the target was a plain tag. A collaborator with Code write access and without Releases write access could permanently delete published releases of that repository, including their attachments. Protected tag rules covering the release tag still blocked the deletion.

CVE-2026-105268.title: The Gitea API routes for issue attachments (`/api/v1/repos/{owner ...
CVE-2026-105268.description: The Gitea API routes for issue attachments (`/api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{index}/assets/{attachment_id}`) also accepted attachments that belong to comments on the issue. Because the author of an issue may edit and delete the issue's attachments, a user who opened an issue could rename or delete attachments that other users had posted in comments on that issue. The contents of the attachments could not be changed.

CVE-2026-105661.title: Requesting `/{username}/-/repositories` for an individual user in ...
CVE-2026-105661.description: Requesting `/{username}/-/repositories` for an individual user instead of an organization made the organization home handler dereference a nil organization and panic. The request needs no authentication and no special configuration. The server answered with an HTTP 500 error and logged a panic for each request; the fix returns 404 for individual users.

CVE-2026-105964.title: The Gitea Actions artifact v4 (Twirp) handlers read the whole req ...
CVE-2026-105964.description: The Gitea Actions artifact v4 (Twirp) handlers read the whole request body into memory without a size limit. A user who can run a workflow and obtains the runner token of that run could send an oversized request to the artifact service and exhaust the memory of the server, which terminates the Gitea process. The request body is now limited to 1 MiB.

CVE-2026-107618.title: `POST /{owner}/{repo}/topics` was registered without the sign-in  ...
CVE-2026-107618.description: `POST /{owner}/{repo}/topics` was registered without the sign-in middleware that provides the cross-origin protection, so a request issued by a third-party site was not rejected. A repository administrator who visited a malicious page could have the topics of their repository changed. No other repository settings were reachable through this route.

CVE-2026-107686.title: The Gitea web handlers for adding and removing reactions on issue ...
CVE-2026-107686.description: The Gitea web handlers for adding and removing reactions on issues and comments did not refuse locked issues for users without write access, although the API did. A signed-in user who could read an issue could therefore add or remove reactions on a locked issue and its comments, bypassing the interaction restriction of the lock. Only reactions were affected; no content could be changed.

CVE-2026-109553.title: Gitea resolved the principals of an SSH certificate by searching  ...
CVE-2026-109553.description: Gitea resolved the principals of an SSH certificate by searching the content of all stored public keys instead of only principal keys. When Gitea trusts a user certificate authority (`SSH_TRUSTED_USER_CA_KEYS`) and accepts arbitrary principals (`SSH_AUTHORIZED_PRINCIPALS_ALLOW=anything`), a user could register another user's public key line as their own principal, or a holder of a certificate signed by that authority could list it, and then authenticate as the owner of that key through the HTTP signature API and the built-in SSH server. Instances that do not trust a user certificate authority are not affected.

CVE-2026-109844.title: `GET /api/v1/user/subscriptions` returned the metadata of every r ...
CVE-2026-109844.description: `GET /api/v1/user/subscriptions` returned the metadata of every repository a user was watching without checking that the user still had access to it. A user who watched a private repository while having access, and later lost it, for example through a team permission downgrade, could still read its name, description, clone URLs, owner and counters. The issue was fixed in 1.27.0 and 28.0.0 and disclosed with 28.2.0.

CVE-2026-110311.title: Creating a draft release through the API returned an `assets` lis ...
CVE-2026-110311.description: Creating a draft release through the API returned an `assets` list that was built from a release without an ID, which matched every attachment that was not linked to a release. A user who could create a draft release in a repository therefore received the metadata (file name, UUID, upload time, size and download count) of issue and comment attachments of repositories they could not read, and of abandoned uploads.

CVE-2026-110324.title: The visibility check of Gitea user profiles was applied to GET re ...
CVE-2026-110324.description: The visibility check of Gitea user profiles was applied to GET requests only, while `POST /{username}` (follow and unfollow) required only a signed-in user. Any authenticated user could therefore obtain the full name, location, website and description of a user with a private profile from the response. The issue was fixed in 28.1.0 and disclosed with 28.2.0.

CVE-2026-110494.title: Adding attachments to a release checked the repository and releas ...
CVE-2026-110494.description: Adding attachments to a release checked the repository and release of an attachment but not whether it was already linked to an issue or comment. A user with write access to the releases of a repository, who knew the UUID of an attachment in that repository, could link it to a release. This exposed the file name, size and download count of the attachment through the release and allowed the user to rename or delete it.

CVE-2026-112887.title: Gitea Actions task tokens authenticate to the REST API as a share ...
CVE-2026-112887.description: Gitea Actions task tokens authenticate to the REST API as a shared system user with a negative ID, which repository, organization, project and key filters treated as having no owner restriction, and the token carried no API scope to restrict user-scoped routes. A user who can run a workflow could use the job's token with `GET /api/v1/user/repos` to list every repository on the instance, including private repositories of other users and organizations, with their metadata. Repository contents remained protected by per-repository permission checks. System users now own nothing, and `/api/v1/user` routes other than `GET /api/v1/user` accept only individual and bot accounts.

CVE-2026-113429.title: Legacy (v1 to v3) Actions artifact uploads stored the request's ` ...
CVE-2026-113429.description: Legacy (v1 to v3) Actions artifact uploads stored the request's `Content-Encoding` header unchecked in the column that is served as the artifact's `Content-Type` on download, and a value starting with `video/` or `audio/` also removed the sandboxing Content-Security-Policy. A user who can run an Actions job could upload an artifact that a browser renders as HTML on the Gitea origin when the direct artifact download URL is opened, and the URL is reachable anonymously on public repositories. A victim who opens the link runs the attacker's script with their own session, which for an administrator means control of the instance. Legacy uploads now store only the `gzip` marker, and the special serve headers are chosen only for valid media types.

CVE-2026-114199.title: `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/heatmap` computed the contribution  ...
CVE-2026-114199.description: `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/heatmap` computed the contribution heatmap with the repository access of the token owner and ignored the public-only restriction of the access token, unlike the activity feed endpoints. A holder of a user's public-only token could read contribution counts and their 15-minute time buckets that stem from that user's activity in private repositories. Repository names and contents were not disclosed. For public-only tokens the heatmap now only counts activity visible to anonymous users.

CVE-2026-116289.title: Gitea did not reject personal access tokens restricted to public  ...
CVE-2026-116289.description: Gitea did not reject personal access tokens restricted to public resources (`public-only`) on the organization Actions runner registration-token endpoint, and the runner registered with the resulting token was not limited to public repositories. Holding only such a token with `write:organization` that belongs to an owner of a public organization, an attacker could register an organization-level runner and receive jobs of the organization's private repositories that have Actions enabled, including the workflow content, Actions secrets and variables, and a task token with access to the private repository. The issue widens what the restricted token can reach; it gives nothing beyond what the owner's full account can already do.

CVE-2026-116296.title: The API routes for releases, release assets, milestones and repos ...
CVE-2026-116296.description: The API routes for releases, release assets, milestones and repository labels did not reject changes to archived repositories. A user with write access to an archived repository, or a holder of such a user's write-scoped token, could replace or delete release assets while keeping their download URLs, delete releases and tags, and create, edit or delete milestones and labels of a repository that is meant to be read-only. Changing requests on these routes now return 423 Locked for archived repositories.

CVE-2026-116474.title: The `GITEA_TOKEN` of a Gitea Actions job authenticates as the `gi ...
CVE-2026-116474.description: The `GITEA_TOKEN` of a Gitea Actions job authenticates as the `gitea-actions` system user, and the `/api/v1/user` email and GPG key endpoints accepted that user, so a job could register an email address and a GPG key on it; without required email confirmation (the default) the address is stored as activated. Commit verification treats a key without a real owner as the instance signing key, so any user who can run a workflow job could make commits signed with their own key show as trusted and signed by the instance in every repository where they appear, including pull requests to repositories the user cannot write to. The impact is limited to the displayed signature status: enforcement such as required signed commits only checks that a signature is verified and is unaffected, and no access is gained. The `/api/v1/user` routes now reject system users.

CVE-2026-117635.title: The `/api/v1/admin` route group did not enforce the `public-only` ...
CVE-2026-117635.description: The `/api/v1/admin` route group did not enforce the `public-only` restriction of personal access tokens. A public-only token with admin scope issued by a site administrator could therefore list private organizations and the email addresses of all users, create organizations, obtain runner registration tokens and create new site administrator accounts, the last of which persists after the token is revoked. Tokens of users who are not site administrators cannot reach these routes; public-only tokens are now rejected on the admin API.

CVE-2026-117646.title: The repositories, stars and watching tabs of user profiles and th ...
CVE-2026-117646.description: The repositories, stars and watching tabs of user profiles and the repository list of organization home pages included private repositories for every signed-in request without checking whether the request used a personal access token restricted to public resources (`public-only`). A holder of such a token could list the private repositories visible to the token's owner, and that user's stars and watches of private repositories. The API and the profile activity tab already applied the restriction. The impact is disclosure of repository names and metadata, not of repository content.

CVE-2026-117649.title: The issue timeline API and the web issue page hid cross-reference ...
CVE-2026-117649.description: The issue timeline API and the web issue page hid cross-reference events that point at issues the reader cannot access, but not "dependency added" and "dependency removed" events. When a readable issue had been linked as a dependency to an issue in a repository the reader cannot access, for example a private repository, any reader of the first issue, including anonymous users of a public repository, received the linked issue's current title, body, state, labels, poster and attachment names through the API, and its repository, number and title on the web page. Creating the link requires access to both issues; comments and attachment downloads of the linked issue stayed protected. Dependency events are now filtered with the same read permission check; a related exposure of unlinked attachment metadata through hidden dependency placeholders was already fixed in 28.2.0.

CVE-2026-117677.title: When parsing an uploaded Helm chart, Gitea decompressed the archi ...
CVE-2026-117677.description: When parsing an uploaded Helm chart, Gitea decompressed the archive and read every tar entry while looking for `Chart.yaml` without limiting the decompressed size, and did so before the package size quota was checked; the quota only considers the compressed upload size. A user with package write access to an owner, for example their own account on an instance with open registration, could repeatedly upload small, highly compressed archives that make the server spend CPU time proportional to the decompressed size, degrading the availability of the Gitea instance. The issue does not allow code execution or data access.

CVE-2026-117685.title: The OCI registry's cross-repository blob mount checked the target ...
CVE-2026-117685.description: The OCI registry's cross-repository blob mount checked the target package against the token's `public-only` restriction, but checked the source blob only against the full account permissions of the token owner. A `public-only` token with `write:package` scope, whose owner can read a private package and write to a public package namespace, could mount a blob of the private package into the public package. The private blob, such as a container layer, could then be downloaded by anyone through the public package.

CVE-2026-118386.title: Workflows triggered by a pull request review were read from the c ...
CVE-2026-118386.description: Workflows triggered by a pull request review were read from the commit named in the review's `commit_id`, while the fork restrictions were decided by the reviewed pull request, and the commit was not checked to belong to that pull request. A user with read access to a repository could place a commit of their own in it, through a fork pull request or an AGit push, and submit a review naming that commit on a pull request whose head branch is in the same repository. On instances with a runner serving the repository, the attacker's workflow then ran without approval, received the Actions secrets of the repository and its owner, and got a `GITEA_TOKEN` with write access to the repository. Review-triggered workflows now run on the pull request head.

CVE-2026-118394.title: The OAuth2 userinfo endpoint (`/login/oauth/userinfo`) decided wh ...
CVE-2026-118394.description: The OAuth2 userinfo endpoint (`/login/oauth/userinfo`) decided whether to limit the `groups` claim to public organizations by re-parsing the `Authorization` header as an OAuth2 access token instead of using the scope of the credential that authenticated the request. When a public-only OAuth2 token was sent as a query parameter or form field, or a public-only personal access token was used, that scope came back empty and the claim listed the token owner's private organizations, teams and concealed memberships. The disclosure is limited to the owner's organization and team names and memberships; no repository content is exposed. The endpoint now uses the scope of the authenticating token.

CVE-2026-118395.title: Gitea 1.27.3 stopped personal access tokens restricted to public  ...
CVE-2026-118395.description: Gitea 1.27.3 stopped personal access tokens restricted to public resources (`public-only`) from creating repositories through `POST /api/v1/user/repos` and `POST /api/v1/repos/migrate`, but `POST /api/v1/org/{org}/repos`, `POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/repos`, `POST /api/v1/orgs` and `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/generate` still accepted such tokens. A holder of a public-only token with the needed write scopes could create private repositories in organizations where the token's owner may create repositories, create private organizations, and generate private repositories from templates. The token still could not read the private repositories it created.

CVE-2026-118504.title: The web interface blocks issue and pull request changes on archiv ...
CVE-2026-118504.description: The web interface blocks issue and pull request changes on archived repositories, but several issue routes of the REST API did not check whether the repository is archived. A user allowed to change issues of an archived repository could use the API to edit, close or delete issues, change labels and deadlines, add or delete tracked time and stopwatches, add reactions, change issue blocks, and pin issues, altering data that archiving is meant to freeze. Gitea 28.2.0 added the check to the issue edit, delete and label routes; Gitea 28.3.0 applies it to all modifying repository API requests.

CVE-2026-119533.title: Repository and organization project boards listed the pull reques ...
CVE-2026-119533.description: Repository and organization project boards listed the pull requests that reference each issue on the board without checking whether the viewer can read them. When a private pull request mentions an issue on a board the viewer can open, the board revealed the private repository's path and the pull request's number, title and state, to anonymous visitors in the case of a public board. The pull request body, diff and files were not exposed. Boards now skip linked pull requests in repositories where the viewer cannot read pull requests.

CVE-2026-119625.title: The `/{username}` web route accepted personal access tokens over  ...
CVE-2026-119625.description: The `/{username}` web route accepted personal access tokens over HTTP Basic authentication without checking their scope. A token confined to an unrelated scope, such as `read:issue`, could read its owner's private activity through the user RSS/Atom feed and the profile activity tab, and other members' activity in a private organization through the organization feed; a public-only token could list the owner's private repositories and organizations and render private profile READMEs. For a site administrator's token this applied to every account. Tokens are now accepted on this route only for feeds, which require `read:user` or `read:organization`.

CVE-2026-119627.title: The web profile and RSS/Atom feed routes of users and organizatio ...
CVE-2026-119627.description: The web profile and RSS/Atom feed routes of users and organizations checked only whether a signed-in viewer could see a limited-visibility owner, without considering the `public-only` restriction of the personal access token used to authenticate. Any user holding a public-only token could send it over HTTP Basic authentication to read the profile and activity feed of limited-visibility users and organizations, which are hidden from anonymous visitors and refused on the equivalent API routes. The disclosure covers existence, profile metadata and public activity; it does not grant write access.

CVE-2026-120263.title: When `[oauth2_client].ACCOUNT_LINKING` is set to `auto` (not the  ...
CVE-2026-120263.description: When `[oauth2_client].ACCOUNT_LINKING` is set to `auto` (not the default) and registration is enabled, the link-account sign-up form looked up the existing account to link by the user name or email submitted in the form instead of the identity asserted by the OAuth2 provider. An attacker with an account on a configured OAuth2 provider could submit another user's name, link their external identity to that Gitea account and be signed in as it without its password, including as an administrator. The link persisted for later sign-ins. Automatic linking now only happens when the existing account matches the provider's email or provider-derived user name; otherwise the account password is required.

CVE-2026-120725.title: Anonymous Git LFS downloads bypass REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW
CVE-2026-120725.description: On an instance with `[service] REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW = true`, the Git LFS routes still serve objects to clients with no account. Anyone who knows a non-private repository's `owner/repo` path and a file's SHA-256 can download that LFS object with `GET /{owner}/{repo}.git/info/lfs/objects/{oid}`. The web UI, the API and `git clone` all refuse the same client. The attached reproducer sets up alice's non-private repository `alice/firmware` with one LFS file, shows the anonymous API request getting 403 and `info/refs` getting 401, and then shows the anonymous LFS GET returning 200 with exactly the bytes alice downloads with her own credentials. The cause is `authenticate()` in `services/lfs/server.go`, reached with `requireSigned = false` from the download, batch, upload and verify handlers. It returns early when the anonymous doer's permission allows reading. The permission model grants `AccessModeRead` to a nil user on any non-private repository of a public owner, and it only consults `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW` for restricted users. The LFS routes are registered with `optSignInFromAnyOrigin`, which carries no `SignInRequired`, so nothing on the LFS path checks the setting. The other read paths (web, API, git smart HTTP, SSH, packages) each check it at their own entry point. The batch route with `'operation': 'download'` also tells an anonymous client whether a given OID is stored in a repository, even without the correct size, since a wrong size returns 422. The attacker cannot discover paths or hashes from the instance; they must come from outside, for example LFS pointer files in a leaked or mirrored checkout or a published checksum. Private repositories and repositories of limited or private owners are not reachable, and write and lock operations still return 401. With `LFS_ALLOW_PURE_SSH = true`, a restricted user or a deploy key of another repository can reach the same objects through `git-lfs-transfer`. This is a second route to the same anonymous read, closed by the same one-line fix. The early return dates from `bbad9b6178` (#5912, 2019). This is the LFS counterpart of the gaps already closed for packages (#20873) and the container registry (#28877). ## Details The Git LFS routes do not honour `[service] REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW = true`. A client without any credential downloads LFS objects from non-private repositories of an instance that otherwise refuses every anonymous read. - Commit: `31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7`. - Attacker: unauthenticated HTTP client that knows `owner/repo` and the SHA-256 (OID) of the object. - Configuration: `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW = true` (default `false`; it is the setting being bypassed) and `LFS_START_SERVER = true` (code default `false`; the web installer writes `true`, `routers/install/install.go:332`). - Entry points: `GET /{owner}/{repo}.git/info/lfs/objects/{oid}` and `POST /{owner}/{repo}.git/info/lfs/objects/batch`. On such an instance, for the non-private repository `alice/firmware` and with no `Authorization` header or cookie: ``` GET /api/v1/repos/alice/firmware -> 403 GET /alice/firmware.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack -> 401 GET /alice/firmware.git/info/lfs/objects/<sha256 of the file> -> 200, the file ``` Every other read path enforces the setting at its own entry point: the web routes through `optSignIn` (`SignInRequired: setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict`, `routers/web/web.go:348`), the API through `verifyAuthWithOptionsAPI` (`routers/api/v1/api.go:1022`), packages in `determineAccessMode` (`services/context/package.go:113`), SSH in `ServCommand` (`routers/private/serv.go:245`), and git smart HTTP with ```go // routers/web/repo/githttp.go:129 // Only public pulls don't need auth: repo must exist, not require-sign-in canAnonymousPull := false if isPull && repoExist && !setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict { ``` The LFS routes have no counterpart. They are registered with `optSignInFromAnyOrigin`, whose `VerifyOptions` carry no `SignInRequired`, because LFS authenticates inside its handlers: ```go // routers/web/web.go:325 var optSignInFromAnyOrigin = verifyAuthWithOptionsWeb(&common.VerifyOptions{DisableCrossOriginProtection: true}) // routers/web/web.go:1764 common.AddOwnerRepoGitLFSRoutes(m, lfsServerEnabled, webAuth.AllowBasic, webAuth.AllowDeployToken, repo.CorsHandler(), optSignInFromAnyOrigin) ``` The handlers reach `authenticate` through `getAuthenticatedRepository`, which passes `requireSigned = false` (`services/lfs/server.go:470`) for the download, batch, upload and verify routes. `authenticate` returns early on the permission of the anonymous doer: ```go // services/lfs/server.go:550 // it works for both anonymous request and signed-in user, then perm.CanAccess will do the permission check perm, err := access_model.GetDoerRepoPermission(ctx, repository, ctx.Doer) // ctx.Doer == nil … canAccess := perm.CanAccess(accessMode, unit.TypeCode) // if it doesn't require sign-in and anonymous user has access, return true … if canAccess && (!requireSigned || ctx.IsSigned) { return true } ``` The comment assumes the permission check covers the anonymous case, but the permission model does not know about the setting for a nil doer: `GetIndividualUserRepoPermission` returns `AccessModeRead` for `user == nil` on any non-private repository whose owner is public (`models/perm/access/repo_permission.go:465-468`). The setting is only consulted there for restricted users (`models/perm/access/access.go:52`). So with no credentials `canAccess` is true for a read, `requireSigned` is false, and the bearer-token check below is never reached. This early return is long-standing, not a recent regression: it dates from `bbad9b6178` ('Fix bug when read public repo lfs file', #5912, 2019-01-31). `DownloadHandler` (`services/lfs/server.go:117`) then streams the object. `BatchHandler` (`:192`) with `'operation': 'download'` answers per OID: a `download` action for an object the repository has, `'error': {'code': 404}` for one it does not have, which lets the same client test whether a given file is stored in a given repository. The size need not be known for this: a wrong size for a stored object is answered with `422` 'Object <oid> is not N bytes' (`services/lfs/server.go:254`), which also confirms presence. The routes that need write access (`batch` with `upload`, `PUT`, `verify`) and the lock routes (`requireSigned = true`, `services/lfs/locks.go:67`) answer 401 to the anonymous client. Presenting credentials can reduce access on the same URL: a restricted user (`gitea admin user create --restricted`) who sends Basic auth gets 401 for the GET above, because the restricted user's permission honours the setting; without the header the answer is 200. The same shortcut is reachable over pure-SSH LFS (`LFS_ALLOW_PURE_SSH = true`, default `false`). The internal LFS routes build a web context that never has a doer (`routers/private/internal.go:105-108`), and `GiteaBackend.Download` requests whatever `{owner}/{repo}.git/info/lfs/…` path the client put into the `id` argument (`modules/lfstransfer/backend/backend.go:185`). This was exercised against the built-in SSH server, separately from the shipped reproducer: a restricted user, and a read-only deploy key of `bob/tool`, are both refused `git-lfs-transfer alice/pub.git download` ('has no 'read' permission for alice/pub'), but inside a `git-lfs-transfer` session on their own repository the packets `get-object <oid>` / `id=base64({'download':{'href':'http://x/alice/pub.git/info/lfs/objects/<oid>'}})` return `status 200` and the file of `alice/pub`. The session's LFS token is bound to the other repository and is never examined. This is a second route to the same anonymous read, not an additional capability: the same person can send the anonymous HTTP request above. The same fix closes both. ## Impact The attacker needs no account, but must already know the repository path and the exact SHA-256 of each file to be read, and the instance reveals neither to an anonymous client. The hash comes from outside: a pointer file in a leaked or mirrored checkout or source archive, a published checksum, or a candidate file whose presence is being tested through the batch route. Only non-private repositories of public owners are reachable (private repositories and repositories of limited or private owners are not), the access is read-only, and it requires the non-default `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW = true`, which is the setting being bypassed. Within those limits: operators set `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW` to make an instance internal, so non-private repositories are meant for every account holder, not for everyone who can reach the HTTP port. LFS objects of those repositories (typically the binaries: firmware images, models, datasets, installers) remain downloadable without an account, while the web pages, the API and git clone refuse the same client. With pure-SSH LFS enabled, restricted users and deploy keys of other repositories reach the same objects through `git-lfs-transfer`, which gives them nothing beyond the anonymous HTTP request. This is the LFS counterpart of gaps already closed for packages (`0a9a86b943`, 'Respect `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW` for packages', #20873) and the container registry (`caad931385`, #28877); unlike those, reading an object here requires knowing its SHA-256. ## Suggested fix The attached patch treats sign-in as required in `authenticate` (`services/lfs/server.go:555-560`) whenever the instance requires it, the same idiom as `routers/api/packages/container/container.go:124`. Requests that carry Basic auth, a session or a deploy token already have `ctx.IsSigned` set by the web auth middleware (`routers/web/web.go:166`); requests with an LFS bearer token fall through to `parseToken` as before. Because every LFS route, including the internal ones used by pure-SSH LFS, goes through this function, the pure-SSH path is covered too. The lock routes already pass `requireSigned = true` and are unaffected. ```diff --- a/services/lfs/server.go +++ b/services/lfs/server.go @@ -555,6 +555,8 @@ func authenticate(ctx *context.Context, repository *repo_model.Repository, autho } canAccess := perm.CanAccess(accessMode, unit.TypeCode) + // the permission model doesn't know 'require sign-in to view', so the anonymous access must be rejected here (the same as git http) + requireSigned = requireSigned || setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict // if it doesn't require sign-in and anonymous user has access, return true // if the user is already signed in (for example: by session auth method), and the doer can access, return true if canAccess && (!requireSigned || ctx.IsSigned) { ``` The patch also adds a regression test, a sub-test of `TestAuthenticate` in `services/lfs/server_test.go` (imports `modules/setting` and `modules/test`): ```go t.Run('authenticate respects require sign-in view', func(t *testing.T) { authenticateAnonymous := func(authorization string) bool { ctx, _ := contexttest.MockContext(t, '/') return authenticate(ctx, repo1, authorization, false, false) } assert.True(t, authenticateAnonymous('')) // public repository defer test.MockVariableValue(&setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict, true)() assert.False(t, authenticateAnonymous('')) assert.True(t, authenticateAnonymous('Bearer '+getUserToken('download', 2, repo1))) }) ``` The sub-test fails without the `server.go` change and `go test ./services/lfs/` passes with it. CVE-2026-123002.title: MFA TOTP brute-force via missing rate limiting on TwoFactorPost (POST /user/two_factor)
CVE-2026-123002.description: **Affected component:** Gitea v1.27.2 (tested `gitea/gitea:latest`), `routers/web/auth/2fa.go` `TwoFactorPost` (POST `/user/two_factor`), backed by `TwoFactor.ValidateAndConsumeTOTP` -> pquerna/otp `totp.Validate` (Skew=1). The scratch-code path `TwoFactorScratchPost` shares the missing control. **Required privileges:** Valid(username + password) for a 2FA-enabled account. ## Summary Gitea lets someone who already knows an account's password guess its second-factor code without limit. The login page never restricts how many wrong 2FA guesses it accepts. An attacker can try codes automatically until one works, then sign in as the victim and turn the second factor off. As only six digits stand between a stolen password and a full login, the second factor provides little real protection. ## Details The route group is registered with only `web.Bind`, no throttle middleware: ```go // routers/web/web.go m.Group('/two_factor', func() { m.Get('', auth.TwoFactor) m.Post('', web.Bind[*forms.TwoFactorAuthForm](), auth.TwoFactorPost) m.Get('/scratch', auth.TwoFactorScratch) m.Post('/scratch', web.Bind[*forms.TwoFactorScratchAuthForm](), auth.TwoFactorScratchPost) }) ``` `TwoFactorPost` branches on the boolean result and, on failure, only re-renders: ```go // routers/web/auth/2fa.go (func TwoFactorPost) ok, err := twofa.ValidateAndConsumeTOTP(ctx, form.Passcode) if err != nil { ctx.ServerError('UserSignIn', err) return } if ok { // ... issue the session, sign in ... } ctx.RenderWithErrDeprecated(ctx.Tr('auth.twofa_passcode_incorrect'), tplTwofa, forms.TwoFactorAuthForm{}) ``` The trailing `RenderWithErrDeprecated` is the entire failure handling: the attempt is not counted and the `twofaUid` session set by the password step stays valid, so the identical POST repeats indefinitely. No web-layer rate limiter exists in `routers/` or `modules/web/` to inherit. Gitea's optional login CAPTCHA (`RequireCaptchaForLogin`) gates only the password step in `SignInPost`; `TwoFactorPost` never calls it, so enabling CAPTCHA does not add a check here. The missing control is the attempt counter, not the crypto. `ValidateAndConsumeTOTP` uses a conditional UPDATE to reject a reused passcode atomically: ```go // models/auth/twofactor.go t.LastUsedPasscode = passcode n, err := db.GetEngine(ctx).ID(t.ID). Where(builder.Or(builder.IsNull{'last_used_passcode'}, builder.Neq{'last_used_passcode': passcode})). Cols('last_used_passcode').Update(t) ... return n == 1, nil ``` `totp.Validate` runs at Skew=1, so 3 of the 1,000,000 codes are valid per 30-second window. Measured observations: - 30 consecutive wrong codes all returned HTTP 200 with no lockout. - Window tolerance confirmed at offsets -1/0/+1 (3 valid codes per 30s window). - The 2FA failure branch emits no log line, so a fail2ban filter watching the log cannot see failed TOTP attempts (that log format exists only in the SSH server, `modules/ssh/ssh.go`). ## Impact An attacker with the password recovers the second factor by exhaustive guessing. With Skew=1, `p = 3 / 1,000,000 ` and expected attempts `1/p = 333,333` (the PoC hit at 309,961). The table uses a conservative 500 req/s, well under the 1,233 req/s the single-client PoC averaged: | Success chance | Attempts | Time @ 500 req/s | |---|---|---| | 50% | 231,049 | 7.7 min | | Mean (63%) | 333,333 | 11.1 min | | 90% | 767,528 | 25.6 min | | 95% | 998,578 | 33.3 min | | 99% | 1,535,057 | 51.2 min | After a hit the attacker holds a fully authenticated session and disables the victim's TOTP. ## Remediation Add an account-keyed failure counter on `twofaUid` and reject once it is exceeded: ```go func TwoFactorPost(ctx *context.Context) { uid, ok := ctx.Session.Get('twofaUid').(int64) if !ok { ctx.ServerError('UserSignIn', errors.New('not in 2FA session')); return } if failedTwoFactor(uid) >= 5 { ctx.RenderWithErrDeprecated(ctx.Tr('auth.twofa_too_many_attempts'), tplTwofa, forms.TwoFactorAuthForm{}) return } ok2, err := twofa.ValidateAndConsumeTOTP(ctx, form.Passcode) // ... on success: resetTwoFactor(uid); sign in ... incrTwoFactor(uid, 5*time.Minute) // 5 failures / 5 minutes, per account ctx.RenderWithErrDeprecated(ctx.Tr('auth.twofa_passcode_incorrect'), tplTwofa, forms.TwoFactorAuthForm{}) } ``` Keying on `twofaUid` means the ceiling cannot be widened by rotating source addresses, and five attempts per five minutes makes a 333,333-guess search infeasible. Defense in depth, independent of the counter: emit a failed-authentication log line on a wrong TOTP in the format Gitea's documented fail2ban filter already matches, so operators who rely on fail2ban gain coverage of the web 2FA path, not just SSH.

CVE-2026-123638.title: Branch protection "Protected file patterns" bypass via git C-quoted file names — push and merge gates both fail open; leads to untrusted Actions workflow execution on self-hosted runners when .gitea/** is protected
CVE-2026-123638.description: ### Summary `GetAffectedFiles` (`modules/git/diff.go`, v28.1.0 lines 303–341) is the **only** file-name source for the branch-protection *Protected file patterns* feature. It runs ```go cmd := gitcmd.NewCommand('diff', '--name-only').AddDynamicArguments(oldCommitID, newCommitID) ... path := strings.TrimSpace(scanner.Text()) // consumed raw — no -z, no C-quote unquoting affectedFiles = append(affectedFiles, path) ``` `git diff --name-only` C-quotes any path containing `'`, `\`, or a control byte, emitting e.g. `'protected/weird\'name.md'` instead of `protected/weird'name.md`. Such a line can never match a pattern like `protected/**` compiled via `glob.Compile(expr, '.', '/')` (`models/git/protected_branch.go:267`), so the protection gate fails **open**. Both enforcement paths consume this function: 1. **Direct push** — `routers/private/hook_pre_receive.go:206-208` → `pull_service.CheckFileProtection` (`services/pull/patch.go:368-381`): ```go affectedFiles, err := git.GetAffectedFiles(...) for _, affectedFile := range affectedFiles { lpath := strings.ToLower(affectedFile) for _, pat := range patterns { if pat.Match(lpath) { ... } // quoted name → no match → not protected ``` 2. **PR merge gate** — `services/pull/patch.go:439` stores `pr.ChangedProtectedFiles` → `services/pull/merge.go:718` `pb.MergeBlockedByProtectedFiles(...)` blocks the merge. Same name source, same blind spot. Meanwhile the **web UI / PR file list** goes through parsers that DO unquote (and #39781, merged 2026-10-15, frames missing unquoting as a bug): the PR view shows the file with its real name and flags it protected, while both enforcement gates let it through — a clean 'UI says protected / enforcement disagrees' divergence. ### Impact A write-access collaborator — precisely the actor this feature exists to constrain — can: 1. **Create or modify** files under any protected pattern by naming them with `'`, `\`, or a control byte. 2. **Destroy existing protected files**: rename `protected/important.yaml` to `protected/gone'x.yaml` (rename detection reports the quoted names; the old, protected-looking name disappears from the affected-file list) and then rewrite/delete its content — verified live. 3. **Execute attacker-chosen code on self-hosted runners** when the owner protects workflow paths (`.gitea/**;.github/**` — the documented pattern for this exact purpose, cf. go-gitea/gitea#33370): a workflow file pushed as `.gitea/workflows/pwn'name.yml` bypasses the gate, is still detected by the Actions workflow scanner, and a run is created and executed by the runner (full 5-hop observed chain in Appendix C; job log line: `PWNED-BY-QUOTED-NAME`). Not affected: **Unprotected file patterns** (the whitelist direction) fails CLOSED — a quoted name there makes the file *more* restricted, not less. Verified. `git fsck --strict` passes these trees; `transfer.fsckObjects` (the duplicate-tree-entry mitigation for CVE-2026-95106) does not block them — quoting is legal git output, not object corruption. ### Suggested fix Make `GetAffectedFiles` consume unquoted paths, exactly as sibling code already does: ```go cmd := gitcmd.NewCommand('diff', '--name-only', '-z').AddDynamicArguments(oldCommitID, newCommitID) // split on NUL; each entry is the raw path — no quoting, no newline ambiguity ``` (the webhook file-list and the Actions `paths:` filter already use `-z`; alternatively unquote with the same helper family that #39781 introduced for `diff-tree --raw`). A regression test should push a `protected/weird'name.md` under `protected/**` and assert rejection. ---

CVE-2026-125423.title: A repository created with auto-init accepted pushes before its in ...
CVE-2026-125423.description: A repository created with auto-init accepted pushes before its initialization had finished, and the initial commit was built in a checkout of whatever the repository already contained. A user who is allowed to create repositories could push a crafted tree during that window so that writing the README followed a symbolic link and overwrote a server-side git hook, which runs commands as the Gitea system user. The initial commit is now built in a freshly initialized directory, and a new repository only becomes ready, and accepts pushes, once its initialization is complete.

CVE-2026-125617.title: User org permissions API leaks hidden org membership and role
CVE-2026-125617.description: Any signed-in Gitea user can find out whether another user is a concealed member of a public or limited organization, and at what level, by calling `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/orgs/{org}/permissions`. The possible answers are owner, admin, write, read, or 'may create repositories'. The routes that normally answer membership questions for outsiders (`/orgs/{org}/members/{username}`, `/orgs/{org}/public_members/{username}` and `/users/{username}/orgs`) give a concealed member the same answer as a non-member. The permissions route tells them apart and adds the role. The attached reproducer runs a default build and queries as a user with no tie to the organization. It gets `is_owner: true` for the organization's concealed creator and `can_read: true` for a concealed read-team member, while the three membership routes return 404 / 404 / `[]` for both. The only access check in `GetUserOrgsPermissions` (`routers/api/v1/org/org.go`) is `HasOrgOrUserVisible` on the organization. After that, the handler returns the target's `GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel`. It never consults `org_user.is_public` or whether the caller is an org member, which is the rule `IsMember`, `ListUserOrgs` and `ListMembers` apply. Because `DEFAULT_ORG_MEMBER_VISIBLE` defaults to false, new memberships start out concealed. The caller needs an account; a token with `read:user` and `read:organization` is enough. Registration is off by default, so on a default instance this means an existing user. What leaks is membership and role only: no repository content and nothing about private organizations. Members of teams with only per-unit permissions are not revealed unless that team can create repositories. For organizations with public repositories, the assignees route already names accounts with write access. The new exposure is therefore mainly organizations without public repositories, read-only members, and exact roles. The private-organization case of this route was fixed in 57b5ed3f25 (#36798), but the per-membership check was never added. Based on a source-level reading of the history, it has been missing since the endpoint was introduced in d0a681fbc3 (#17232), first released in v1.16.0-rc1. ## Details `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/orgs/{org}/permissions` tells any signed-in user what role `{username}` holds in `{org}`, including when that membership is not public. Scanned commit: `31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7`. Attacker position: a regular user with no relation to the organization. Configuration: default. Observed on the stock build with default settings, as user `attacker`, against the public organization `victimorg` whose creator `orgowner` and team member `hiddenmember` both have `org_user.is_public = false`, and against `bystander`, who is not a member: | request (as `attacker`) | `orgowner` | `hiddenmember` | `bystander` | |---|---|---|---| | `GET /orgs/victimorg/members/{user}` | 303 → `public_members` → 404 | 303 → 404 | 303 → 404 | | `GET /orgs/victimorg/public_members/{user}` | 404 | 404 | 404 | | `GET /users/{user}/orgs` | `[]` | `[]` | `[]` | | `GET /users/{user}/orgs/victimorg/permissions` | 200, `is_owner: true` (all five fields true) | 200, `can_read: true` | 200, all five fields false | The three routes that answer 'is this user a member' give an outsider the same answer for a concealed member and a non-member. The permissions route separates them and adds the role. The handler's only visibility check is on the organization: ```go // routers/api/v1/org/org.go:157-163 if !organization.HasOrgOrUserVisible(ctx, o, ctx.Doer) { ctx.APIErrorNotFound() return } org := organization.OrgFromUser(o) authorizeLevel, err := org.GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel(ctx, ctx.ContextUser.ID) ``` `GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel` (`models/organization/org.go:416`) is `max(team.authorize)` over the target's `team_user` rows in the org. Lines 169-186 translate it into `can_read` / `can_write` / `is_admin` / `is_owner` and add `can_create_repository` from `CanCreateOrgRepo`. Neither `org_user.is_public` for the target nor the caller's own membership is consulted anywhere on the path. The route is registered at `routers/api/v1/api.go:1776-1779`. Its guards are `reqToken()`, the token scopes `read:user` and `read:organization` (a token with exactly these two scopes gets the same 200 responses), `checkTokenPublicOnly()`, and `individualPermsChecker` (`api.go:984`), which only requires that `{username}` is visible to the caller. An anonymous request gets 401. The siblings do apply the membership rule: - `IsMember` (`routers/api/v1/org/member.go:153-175`) answers directly only when the caller is an org member or a site admin; everyone else is redirected to `public_members`, and `IsPublicMember` (`member.go:204`) answers from `organization.IsPublicMembership`. - `ListUserOrgs` goes through `queryUserOrgIDs` (`models/organization/org_list.go:63-69`), which adds `is_public = true` unless the caller is the user or an admin. - `ListMembers` uses `FindOrgMembersOpts.PublicOnly()` (`models/organization/org.go:180`) to restrict non-members to public memberships. Memberships start out concealed: both `CreateOrganization` (`models/organization/org.go:350`) and `AddOrgUser` (`org.go:532`) insert the `org_user` row with `IsPublic: setting.Service.DefaultOrgMemberVisible`, and `[service] DEFAULT_ORG_MEMBER_VISIBLE` defaults to `false` (`modules/setting/service.go:244`). What the response reveals depends on `team.authorize`: - The Owners team has `authorize = owner`, so every concealed owner comes back with `is_owner: true`. - Teams with a general permission reveal their members as `can_read` / `can_write` / `is_admin`. `POST /orgs/{org}/teams` with `permission` and no `units`/`units_map` creates such a team for `read`, `write` or `admin` (`routers/api/v1/org/team.go:177-181`); the web form handler does for `write` and `admin` (`routers/web/org/teams.go:347`). Read and write teams created through the API were observed; the admin case follows from the same comparisons in the handler, and the web-form path was read from source, not run. - Teams defined per unit have `authorize = none` (`team.go:170`, `routers/web/org/teams.go:370`). A member of only such teams returns the same all-false body as a non-member, unless the team has `can_create_org_repo`, in which case `can_create_repository: true` gives the membership away. Both cases were observed on the running server. A limited organization behaves like a public one for a signed-in caller (observed: 200 with `is_owner: true`). A private organization returns 404 to non-members; that case was closed by 57b5ed3f25 (#36798), which made `HasOrgOrUserVisible` test the caller instead of the target. The per-membership check is the part that is still missing; it has been absent since the endpoint was added in `d0a681fbc3fb` ('[API] Add endpount to get user org permissions (#17232)', 2021-10-12), first released in v1.16.0-rc1. ## Impact The attacker needs an account, and what leaks is membership and role metadata only: no repository content, and nothing about private organizations. Registration is disabled by default (`DISABLE_REGISTRATION` defaults to `true`, `modules/setting/service.go:148`), so on a default instance this is an existing user; on instances with open registration it is anyone. With that, any signed-in user can test any visible username against any public or limited organization and learn whether that user is a concealed owner, or a concealed member of an admin/write/read team or of a team that may create repositories, together with that role. Iterating over usernames lists the concealed members of such an organization with their roles. This defeats the membership-visibility setting that the other organization routes enforce. That concealment is already partial elsewhere. When the organization owns a public repository, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/assignees` lists the accounts with write access to that repository to any signed-in user (observed on the same instance: it returned the concealed owner and a concealed write-team member), and issue comments label a concealed member's posts as Owner/Member (from source, not run). What the permissions route adds is organizations without public repositories, read-only members, and the exact role. ## Suggested fix The attached patch applies the rule `IsMember` already uses. In `GetUserOrgsPermissions` (`routers/api/v1/org/org.go`), right after `organization.OrgFromUser(o)` and before `GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel`, it checks who is asking. If the caller is not the target user and not a site admin, the patch checks whether the caller is a member of the organization (`org.IsOrgMember`). If not, the target's membership must be public (`organization.IsPublicMembership`), and otherwise the handler returns `ctx.APIErrorNotFound()`. A non-public membership therefore gets the same 404 as a non-membership, so the two stay indistinguishable, and this is the same 404 the other membership routes give. This changes the answer an outsider gets for a non-member from `200` with all fields false to `404`. Answers for self, site-admin and fellow-member queries are unchanged, and the existing `TestPermissionsAPI` cases, which all query as self or admin, still pass. If the 200 shape has to stay, returning the zero-valued `OrganizationPermissions` in that branch closes the leak equally. The patch also adds a regression subtest, `testHiddenMemberOfPublicOrg`, run from `TestPermissionsAPI` in `tests/integration/api_user_org_perm_test.go`. It uses the fixtures: org3 is public, user2's membership is public, user4's is not, and user5 and user8 are not members. As user8 it expects 404 for user4 and user5 and 200 with `is_owner` for user2. As user2 (a member) it expects 200 with `can_write` for user4. The test fails on the unpatched handler and passes with the patch. ## Suggested patch ```diff diff --git a/routers/api/v1/org/org.go b/routers/api/v1/org/org.go index ed450d21e9..46f5311723 100644 --- a/routers/api/v1/org/org.go +++ b/routers/api/v1/org/org.go @@ -160,6 +160,29 @@ func GetUserOrgsPermissions(ctx *context.APIContext) { } org := organization.OrgFromUser(o) + + // Like IsMember: a non-public membership is only disclosed to the user themselves, + // to site admins and to members of the organization. Everyone else gets the same + // 404 as for a non-member, so hidden members stay indistinguishable from non-members. + if ctx.Doer.ID != ctx.ContextUser.ID && !ctx.Doer.IsAdmin { + doerIsMember, err := org.IsOrgMember(ctx, ctx.Doer.ID) + if err != nil { + ctx.APIErrorInternal(err) + return + } + if !doerIsMember { + isPublicMember, err := organization.IsPublicMembership(ctx, org.ID, ctx.ContextUser.ID) + if err != nil { + ctx.APIErrorInternal(err) + return + } + if !isPublicMember { + ctx.APIErrorNotFound() + return + } + } + } + authorizeLevel, err := org.GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel(ctx, ctx.ContextUser.ID) if err != nil { ctx.APIErrorInternal(err) diff --git a/tests/integration/api_user_org_perm_test.go b/tests/integration/api_user_org_perm_test.go index 63d69fab71..7cdfa233dd 100644 --- a/tests/integration/api_user_org_perm_test.go +++ b/tests/integration/api_user_org_perm_test.go @@ -28,6 +28,7 @@ func TestPermissionsAPI(t *testing.T) { t.Run('UnknownOrganization', testUnknownOrganization) t.Run('HiddenMemberPermissionsForbidden', testHiddenMemberPermissionsForbidden) t.Run('PrivateOrgPermissionsNotFound', testPrivateOrgPermissionsNotFound) + t.Run('HiddenMemberOfPublicOrg', testHiddenMemberOfPublicOrg) } type apiUserOrgPermTestCase struct { @@ -179,6 +180,35 @@ func testHiddenMemberPermissionsForbidden(t *testing.T) { }, apiOP) } +func testHiddenMemberOfPublicOrg(t *testing.T) { + // org3 is public; user2's membership is public, user4's is not, user5 and user8 are not members + outsiderSession := loginUser(t, 'user8') + outsiderToken := getTokenForLoggedInUser(t, outsiderSession, auth_model.AccessTokenScopeReadUser, auth_model.AccessTokenScopeReadOrganization) + + // a hidden membership must look like a non-membership to an outsider + req := NewRequest(t, 'GET', '/api/v1/users/user4/orgs/org3/permissions'). + AddTokenAuth(outsiderToken) + MakeRequest(t, req, http.StatusNotFound) + req = NewRequest(t, 'GET', '/api/v1/users/user5/orgs/org3/permissions'). + AddTokenAuth(outsiderToken) + MakeRequest(t, req, http.StatusNotFound) + + // a public membership is still visible to an outsider + req = NewRequest(t, 'GET', '/api/v1/users/user2/orgs/org3/permissions'). + AddTokenAuth(outsiderToken) + resp := MakeRequest(t, req, http.StatusOK) + assert.True(t, DecodeJSON(t, resp, &api.OrganizationPermissions{}).IsOwner) + + // an org member can see the hidden membership + memberSession := loginUser(t, 'user2') + memberToken := getTokenForLoggedInUser(t, memberSession, auth_model.AccessTokenScopeReadUser, auth_model.AccessTokenScopeReadOrganization) + + req = NewRequest(t, 'GET', '/api/v1/users/user4/orgs/org3/permissions'). + AddTokenAuth(memberToken) + resp = MakeRequest(t, req, http.StatusOK) + assert.True(t, DecodeJSON(t, resp, &api.OrganizationPermissions{}).CanWrite) +} + func testPrivateOrgPermissionsNotFound(t *testing.T) { session := loginUser(t, 'user8') token := getTokenForLoggedInUser(t, session, auth_model.AccessTokenScopeReadUser, auth_model.AccessTokenScopeReadOrganization) ``` _Reported by the Anthropic OSS scanner, finding ANT-2026-122LRIRU (scan gitea-20261022-004), commit 31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7._

CVE-2026-126338.title: Code comment reply accepts foreign review ID, leaks private diff hunks
CVE-2026-126338.description:
A missing authorization check in Gitea's code-comment reply path lets any signed-in regular user read diff hunks from pull requests in private repositories they have no access to. By submitting a reply whose `reply` form field names a review from another repository, the attacker gets that review's stored diff hunk and commit SHA copied into a comment on a pull request they can comment on. The hunk is up to `[ui] CODE_COMMENT_LINES` diff lines, 4 by default, ending at the commented line. On default settings, the attached reproducer recovers a `PASSWORD=s3cr3t-of-the-victim` line from `victim/private`, while the same attacker gets 404 when asking the API for that review's comments directly. The bug is in `createCodeComment` in `services/pull/review.go`. When `reviewID != 0`, it calls `FindComments` with only `ReviewID`, `Line`, `TreePath` and `Type`, with no `IssueID` or `RepoID`. It then copies the first match's `Patch`, `CommitSHA` and `Invalidated` into the new comment. The caller, `pull_service.CreateCodeComment`, only checks that the caller's own pull request already has a code comment on that path and line. It never checks that `replyReviewID` belongs to that pull request. The attacker first comments on the matching path and line in a pull request they can comment on (they do not need a repository of their own). They then post the reply form to `POST /{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/files/reviews/comments`, and read the copied `diff_hunk` back by replying to the planted comment through the API. The leak is narrow. Each hit needs a review ID, which is sequential instance-wide but does not reveal its repository. It also needs the exact file path and line of a review comment on the new side of the diff, although the response status confirms guesses (200 for a hit, 500 for a wrong path or line, 404 for a nonexistent review). Pending reviews are affected too, but only the diff under a draft comment leaks, not the draft text. The unbound lookup was introduced in b091c994b593 ('Comments on review should have the same sha (#13448)') and first released in v1.14.0. The API reply route used here to read the hunk back exists only since v1.27.0, so on older releases the hunk is still copied but cannot be read back this way. ## Details When a code comment is posted as a reply, `createCodeComment` reuses the diff hunk stored with the first comment of the review being replied to. The review ID is the form field `reply`, and the lookup is not limited to the pull request (or repository) the request was authorized for: ```go // services/pull/review.go:218 if line > 0 { if reviewID != 0 { first, err := issues_model.FindComments(ctx, &issues_model.FindCommentsOptions{ ReviewID: reviewID, // request-controlled; no IssueID, no RepoID Line: line, TreePath: treePath, Type: issues_model.CommentTypeCode, … }) if err == nil && len(first) > 0 { commitID = first[0].CommitSHA invalidated = first[0].Invalidated patch = first[0].Patch // diff hunk of whatever repository that review belongs to } … ``` Observed at commit `31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7` with default settings: `victim/private` is a private repository whose pull request changes line 3 of `deploy/settings.env` to `PASSWORD=s3cr3t-of-the-victim`; review 1 has a comment on that line. The unrelated regular user `attacker` opens a pull request in their own `attacker/scratch`, comments on `deploy/settings.env` line 3 there, and submits the reply form with `reply=1`. The API then hands the attacker a comment in `attacker/scratch` with ``` 'diff_hunk': '@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 HOST=db.internal
 USER=app
-PASSWORD=
+PASSWORD=s3cr3t-of-the-victim' ``` and the `commit_id` of the victim's commit, while `GET /api/v1/repos/victim/private/pulls/1/reviews/1/comments` answers the attacker 404. The path from the request to the copy: 1. `POST /{username}/{reponame}/pulls/{index}/files/reviews/comments` (`routers/web/web.go:1662`) sits behind `context.RepoMustNotBeArchived()` (`:1664`) and `optSignIn, context.RepoAssignment, repo.MustAllowPulls, reqUnitPullsReader` (`:1667`). All of them look at the repository in the URL, which can be the attacker's own. 2. `repo.CreateCodeComment` (`routers/web/repo/pull_review.go:64`) loads the pull request from the URL with `GetActionIssue` and passes `form.Reply` (`services/forms/repo_form.go:471`) unchecked as `replyReviewID` (`:98`). In the UI the field is filled by `templates/repo/diff/comment_form.tmpl:34` with the review ID of the conversation being replied to. 3. `pull_service.CreateCodeComment` (`services/pull/review.go:119-125`) asks only `ReviewExists(ctx, issue, treePath, line)` (`models/issues/review.go:451`): does the *caller's* pull request already have a code comment on that path and line? The attacker creates that comment first; the path does not have to exist in their pull request. `replyReviewID` is never compared with `issue.ID`. 4. `createCodeComment(…, replyReviewID, …)` runs the lookup quoted above. `FindCommentsOptions.ToConds` (`models/issues/comment.go:1094-1119`) adds a repository or issue condition only when `RepoID` / `IssueID` are set, so the query is `review_id = ? AND line = ? AND tree_path = ? AND type = code` over all repositories. The new comment is then created on the caller's pull request with `CommitSHA: commitID`, `ReviewID: reviewID`, `Patch: patch` (`services/pull/review.go:287-300`). 5. Reading it back: the form's HTML response renders the conversation with the hunk of its first comment (the attacker's own). The stored hunk is exposed as `diff_hunk` / `commit_id` by `convert.ToPullReviewComment` (`services/convert/pull_review.go:113-115`). `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/comments/{id}/replies` (`CreatePullReviewCommentReply`, `routers/api/v1/repo/pull_review.go:209`) returns that JSON for the reply it creates. This route cannot name a foreign review by itself, because it loads the parent comment with `GetCommentWithRepoID(ctx, ctx.Repo.Repository.ID, …)` and takes `parent.ReviewID`; but the comment planted in step 4 is in the attacker's repository and carries the foreign `ReviewID`, so a reply to it goes through the same unbound lookup and returns the victim's hunk. The unbound lookup was introduced in `b091c994b593` ('Comments on review should have the same sha (#13448)', 2020-11-09) and first released in v1.14.0. The API reply route used in step 5 to read the hunk back only exists since v1.27.0 (`331450b17a`, 2026-04-27), so on older releases the hunk is still copied into the attacker's comment but this way of reading it back is not available. The notification mail template (`templates/mail/repo/issue/default.tmpl:56`) also prints the stored hunk; that channel was not tested (no mail offline). Other users of a request-supplied review ID bind it: `DismissReview` compares `review.Issue.RepoID` with the repository (`services/pull/review.go:420-423`), and the API's `prepareSingleReview` rejects `review.IssueID != pr.IssueID` and pending reviews of other users (`routers/api/v1/repo/pull_review.go:722-732`). ## Impact A signed-in regular user on a default configuration reads diff hunks of pull requests in repositories they have no access to, within narrow limits: each hit yields at most the last `[ui] CODE_COMMENT_LINES` (default 4) diff lines ending at a line that carries a review comment, plus the commit SHA; only comments on the new side of the diff are reachable (the lookup runs for `line > 0`); and for each hunk the attacker must supply the review ID, the exact file path and the line. They need one pull request they can comment on. No repository of their own is needed: a third account with no repository got the same result (HTTP 200) on somebody else's public pull request, once a code comment existed on that path and line there. Review IDs are one auto-increment sequence for the whole instance, so the attacker's own reviews reveal the current range, but an ID does not tell which repository its review belongs to, so the leak cannot be aimed at one chosen repository. Path and line have to be known (former collaborator, private fork of a public project, conventional file names) or guessed; each guess costs two requests (the comment on that path and line in the attacker's pull request, then the reply) and the reply's status confirms it. Observed: 200 for a hit, 500 for a wrong path or line on an existing foreign review (`git blame` is run on that review's commit ID in the attacker's repository and fails with `bad object`), 404 for a review ID that does not exist; the two misses create no comment. The copy also happens for a review that is still pending: a reply naming the victim's unsubmitted review stored the diff hunk under its draft comment in the attacker's comment, and an API reply to that comment returned it. What leaks is the diff under the draft, not the draft comment's text. In that case the planted comment is not rendered in the form's response, so its ID has to be derived from the sequential comment IDs; this step was checked with the ID taken from the database and is not part of the reproducer. As a side effect the attacker's comment row points to a review of another repository (`comment.review_id`). ## Suggested fix The attached patch checks the caller-supplied review ID in `pull_service.CreateCodeComment`, the one service function both the web reply form and the API reply endpoint go through. It loads the review and rejects it with `ErrReviewNotExist` unless it is a review of the pull request being commented on and, if still pending, belongs to the doer (as `prepareSingleReview` does), and it additionally binds the lookup in `createCodeComment` to the issue: ```diff --- a/services/pull/review.go +++ b/services/pull/review.go @@ -117,6 +117,15 @@ func CreateCodeComment( if !pendingReview && replyReviewID != 0 { + // The review ID is provided by the caller, make sure it is a review of this pull request which the doer can see + replyReview, err := issues_model.GetReviewByID(ctx, replyReviewID) + if err != nil { + return nil, err + } + if replyReview.IssueID != issue.ID || (replyReview.Type == issues_model.ReviewTypePending && replyReview.ReviewerID != doer.ID) { + return nil, issues_model.ErrReviewNotExist{ID: replyReviewID} + } + // It's not part of a review; maybe a reply to a review comment or a single comment. @@ -218,6 +227,7 @@ func createCodeComment( first, err := issues_model.FindComments(ctx, &issues_model.FindCommentsOptions{ + IssueID: issue.ID, ReviewID: reviewID, ``` The web handler needs no change: `ctx.ServerError` already answers 404 for errors wrapping `util.ErrNotExist` (`services/context/context_response.go:170`). In `CreatePullReviewCommentReply` the patch routes the error through `ctx.APIErrorAuto(err)` instead of `ctx.APIErrorInternal(err)`, so a rejected review yields 404 instead of 500. A reply naming a nonexistent or foreign review is refused and no comment is created; replies to a review of the same pull request are unaffected. Unlike `prepareSingleReview`, there is no exception for site admins on other users' pending reviews. The patch adds a regression test, `TestCreateCodeCommentReplyReview` in `services/pull/review_test.go`, that calls `pull_service.CreateCodeComment` with the ID of a review created on a pull request of another repository (fixtures: issue 3 as the caller's, issue 12 as the foreign one), with another user's pending review of the same pull request, and with a non-existent ID, each expecting `IsErrReviewNotExist` and no comment created; a reply to a review of the same pull request still succeeds and inherits its patch. With the patch applied the reproducer prints `OK`. Comment rows already planted on a live instance keep the copied hunk; code comments whose `review_id` belongs to a review of a different issue identify past abuse. ## Suggested patch ```diff diff
