On such an instance, for the non-private repository `alice/firmware` and with no `Authorization` header or cookie: ``` GET /api/v1/repos/alice/firmware -> 403 GET /alice/firmware.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack -> 401 GET /alice/firmware.git/info/lfs/objects/<sha256 of the file> -> 200, the file ``` Every other read path enforces the setting at its own entry point: the web routes through `optSignIn` (`SignInRequired: setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict`, `routers/web/web.go:348`), the API through `verifyAuthWithOptionsAPI` (`routers/api/v1/api.go:1022`), packages in `determineAccessMode` (`services/context/package.go:113`), SSH in `ServCommand` (`routers/private/serv.go:245`), and git smart HTTP with ```go // routers/web/repo/githttp.go:129 // Only public pulls don't need auth: repo must exist, not require-sign-in canAnonymousPull := false if isPull && repoExist && !setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict { ``` The LFS routes have no counterpart. They are registered with `optSignInFromAnyOrigin`, whose `VerifyOptions` carry no `SignInRequired`, because LFS authenticates inside its handlers: ```go // routers/web/web.go:325 var optSignInFromAnyOrigin = verifyAuthWithOptionsWeb(&common.VerifyOptions{DisableCrossOriginProtection: true}) // routers/web/web.go:1764 common.AddOwnerRepoGitLFSRoutes(m, lfsServerEnabled, webAuth.AllowBasic, webAuth.AllowDeployToken, repo.CorsHandler(), optSignInFromAnyOrigin) ``` The handlers reach `authenticate` through `getAuthenticatedRepository`, which passes `requireSigned = false` (`services/lfs/server.go:470`) for the download, batch, upload and verify routes. `authenticate` returns early on the permission of the anonymous doer: ```go // services/lfs/server.go:550 // it works for both anonymous request and signed-in user, then perm.CanAccess will do the permission check perm, err := access_model.GetDoerRepoPermission(ctx, repository, ctx.Doer) // ctx.Doer == nil … canAccess := perm.CanAccess(accessMode, unit.TypeCode) // if it doesn't require sign-in and anonymous user has access, return true … if canAccess && (!requireSigned || ctx.IsSigned) { return true } ``` The comment assumes the permission check covers the anonymous case, but the permission model does not know about the setting for a nil doer: `GetIndividualUserRepoPermission` returns `AccessModeRead` for `user == nil` on any non-private repository whose owner is public (`models/perm/access/repo_permission.go:465-468`). The setting is only consulted there for restricted users (`models/perm/access/access.go:52`). So with no credentials `canAccess` is true for a read, `requireSigned` is false, and the bearer-token check below is never reached. This early return is long-standing, not a recent regression: it dates from `bbad9b6178` ('Fix bug when read public repo lfs file', #5912, 2019-01-31). `DownloadHandler` (`services/lfs/server.go:117`) then streams the object. `BatchHandler` (`:192`) with `'operation': 'download'` answers per OID: a `download` action for an object the repository has, `'error': {'code': 404}` for one it does not have, which lets the same client test whether a given file is stored in a given repository. The size need not be known for this: a wrong size for a stored object is answered with `422` 'Object <oid> is not N bytes' (`services/lfs/server.go:254`), which also confirms presence. The routes that need write access (`batch` with `upload`, `PUT`, `verify`) and the lock routes (`requireSigned = true`, `services/lfs/locks.go:67`) answer 401 to the anonymous client. Presenting credentials can reduce access on the same URL: a restricted user (`gitea admin user create --restricted`) who sends Basic auth gets 401 for the GET above, because the restricted user's permission honours the setting; without the header the answer is 200. The same shortcut is reachable over pure-SSH LFS (`LFS_ALLOW_PURE_SSH = true`, default `false`). The internal LFS routes build a web context that never has a doer (`routers/private/internal.go:105-108`), and `GiteaBackend.Download` requests whatever `{owner}/{repo}.git/info/lfs/…` path the client put into the `id` argument (`modules/lfstransfer/backend/backend.go:185`). This was exercised against the built-in SSH server, separately from the shipped reproducer: a restricted user, and a read-only deploy key of `bob/tool`, are both refused `git-lfs-transfer alice/pub.git download` ('has no 'read' permission for alice/pub'), but inside a `git-lfs-transfer` session on their own repository the packets `get-object <oid>` / `id=base64({'download':{'href':'http://x/alice/pub.git/info/lfs/objects/<oid>'}})` return `status 200` and the file of `alice/pub`. The session's LFS token is bound to the other repository and is never examined. This is a second route to the same anonymous read, not an additional capability: the same person can send the anonymous HTTP request above. The same fix closes both. ## Impact The attacker needs no account, but must already know the repository path and the exact SHA-256 of each file to be read, and the instance reveals neither to an anonymous client. The hash comes from outside: a pointer file in a leaked or mirrored checkout or source archive, a published checksum, or a candidate file whose presence is being tested through the batch route. Only non-private repositories of public owners are reachable (private repositories and repositories of limited or private owners are not), the access is read-only, and it requires the non-default `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW = true`, which is the setting being bypassed. Within those limits: operators set `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW` to make an instance internal, so non-private repositories are meant for every account holder, not for everyone who can reach the HTTP port. LFS objects of those repositories (typically the binaries: firmware images, models, datasets, installers) remain downloadable without an account, while the web pages, the API and git clone refuse the same client. With pure-SSH LFS enabled, restricted users and deploy keys of other repositories reach the same objects through `git-lfs-transfer`, which gives them nothing beyond the anonymous HTTP request. This is the LFS counterpart of gaps already closed for packages (`0a9a86b943`, 'Respect `REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW` for packages', #20873) and the container registry (`caad931385`, #28877); unlike those, reading an object here requires knowing its SHA-256. ## Suggested fix The attached patch treats sign-in as required in `authenticate` (`services/lfs/server.go:555-560`) whenever the instance requires it, the same idiom as `routers/api/packages/container/container.go:124`. Requests that carry Basic auth, a session or a deploy token already have `ctx.IsSigned` set by the web auth middleware (`routers/web/web.go:166`); requests with an LFS bearer token fall through to `parseToken` as before. Because every LFS route, including the internal ones used by pure-SSH LFS, goes through this function, the pure-SSH path is covered too. The lock routes already pass `requireSigned = true` and are unaffected. ```diff --- a/services/lfs/server.go +++ b/services/lfs/server.go @@ -555,6 +555,8 @@ func authenticate(ctx *context.Context, repository *repo_model.Repository, autho } canAccess := perm.CanAccess(accessMode, unit.TypeCode) + // the permission model doesn't know 'require sign-in to view', so the anonymous access must be rejected here (the same as git http) + requireSigned = requireSigned || setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict // if it doesn't require sign-in and anonymous user has access, return true // if the user is already signed in (for example: by session auth method), and the doer can access, return true if canAccess && (!requireSigned || ctx.IsSigned) { ``` The patch also adds a regression test, a sub-test of `TestAuthenticate` in `services/lfs/server_test.go` (imports `modules/setting` and `modules/test`): ```go t.Run('authenticate respects require sign-in view', func(t *testing.T) { authenticateAnonymous := func(authorization string) bool { ctx, _ := contexttest.MockContext(t, '/') return authenticate(ctx, repo1, authorization, false, false) } assert.True(t, authenticateAnonymous('')) // public repository defer test.MockVariableValue(&setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict, true)() assert.False(t, authenticateAnonymous('')) assert.True(t, authenticateAnonymous('Bearer '+getUserToken('download', 2, repo1))) }) ``` The sub-test fails without the `server.go` change and `go test ./services/lfs/` passes with it. With the patch the reproducer prints `OK`, a regular user's Basic-auth download still returns 200, the two SSH cases above return `status 401`, and the repository owner's `batch` + `get-object` over `git-lfs-transfer` still return the file. Independently, and not part of the attached patch, `GiteaBackend.Download`, `Upload` and `Verify` (`modules/lfstransfer/backend/backend.go:185`, `:239`, `:286`) could build the internal URL from `g.server` (the repository the SSH session was authorized for) and the OID instead of taking the repository path from the client's `id` argument. ## Suggested patch ```diff diff --git a/services/lfs/server.go b/services/lfs/server.go index 6d5df20b12..6395db57e3 100644 --- a/services/lfs/server.go +++ b/services/lfs/server.go @@ -555,6 +555,8 @@ func authenticate(ctx *context.Context, repository *repo_model.Repository, autho } canAccess := perm.CanAccess(accessMode, unit.TypeCode) + // the permission model doesn't know 'require sign-in to view', so the anonymous access must be rejected here (the same as git http) + requireSigned = requireSigned || setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict // if it doesn't require sign-in and anonymous user has access, return true // if the user is already signed in (for example: by session auth method), and the doer can access, return true if canAccess && (!requireSigned || ctx.IsSigned) { diff --git a/services/lfs/server_test.go b/services/lfs/server_test.go index 8ccf777caf..88b0b4792d 100644 --- a/services/lfs/server_test.go +++ b/services/lfs/server_test.go @@ -13,6 +13,8 @@ import ( repo_model 'gitea.dev/models/repo' 'gitea.dev/models/unittest' user_model 'gitea.dev/models/user' + 'gitea.dev/modules/setting' + 'gitea.dev/modules/test' 'gitea.dev/services/contexttest' 'github.com/stretchr/testify/assert' @@ -57,6 +59,18 @@ func TestAuthenticate(t *testing.T) { assert.True(t, authenticate(ctx, repo1, prefixBearer+token, true, false)) }) + t.Run('authenticate respects require sign-in view', func(t *testing.T) { + authenticateAnonymous := func(authorization string) bool { + ctx, _ := contexttest.MockContext(t, '/') + return authenticate(ctx, repo1, authorization, false, false) + } + assert.True(t, authenticateAnonymous('')) // public repository + + defer test.MockVariableValue(&setting.Service.RequireSignInViewStrict, true)() + assert.False(t, authenticateAnonymous('')) + assert.True(t, authenticateAnonymous('Bearer '+getUserToken('download', 2, repo1))) + }) + handleLFSTokenTestPerm := func(op string, userID int64, repo *repo_model.Repository, accessMode perm_model.AccessMode) error { token := getUserToken(op, userID, repo) u, err := handleLFSToken(ctx, token, repo, accessMode) ``` _Reported by the Anthropic OSS scanner, finding ANT-2026-1XWM1MVI (scan gitea-20261022-004), commit 31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7._

CVE-2026-123002.title: MFA TOTP brute-force via missing rate limiting on TwoFactorPost (POST /user/two_factor)
CVE-2026-123002.description: **Affected component:** Gitea v1.27.2 (tested `gitea/gitea:latest`), `routers/web/auth/2fa.go` `TwoFactorPost` (POST `/user/two_factor`), backed by `TwoFactor.ValidateAndConsumeTOTP` -> pquerna/otp `totp.Validate` (Skew=1). The scratch-code path `TwoFactorScratchPost` shares the missing control. **Required privileges:** Valid(username + password) for a 2FA-enabled account. ## Summary Gitea lets someone who already knows an account's password guess its second-factor code without limit. The login page never restricts how many wrong 2FA guesses it accepts. An attacker can try codes automatically until one works, then sign in as the victim and turn the second factor off. As only six digits stand between a stolen password and a full login, the second factor provides little real protection. ## Details The route group is registered with only `web.Bind`, no throttle middleware: ```go // routers/web/web.go m.Group('/two_factor', func() { m.Get('', auth.TwoFactor) m.Post('', web.Bind[*forms.TwoFactorAuthForm](), auth.TwoFactorPost) m.Get('/scratch', auth.TwoFactorScratch) m.Post('/scratch', web.Bind[*forms.TwoFactorScratchAuthForm](), auth.TwoFactorScratchPost) }) ``` `TwoFactorPost` branches on the boolean result and, on failure, only re-renders: ```go // routers/web/auth/2fa.go (func TwoFactorPost) ok, err := twofa.ValidateAndConsumeTOTP(ctx, form.Passcode) if err != nil { ctx.ServerError('UserSignIn', err) return } if ok { // ... issue the session, sign in ... } ctx.RenderWithErrDeprecated(ctx.Tr('auth.twofa_passcode_incorrect'), tplTwofa, forms.TwoFactorAuthForm{}) ``` The trailing `RenderWithErrDeprecated` is the entire failure handling: the attempt is not counted and the `twofaUid` session set by the password step stays valid, so the identical POST repeats indefinitely. No web-layer rate limiter exists in `routers/` or `modules/web/` to inherit. Gitea's optional login CAPTCHA (`RequireCaptchaForLogin`) gates only the password step in `SignInPost`; `TwoFactorPost` never calls it, so enabling CAPTCHA does not add a check here. The missing control is the attempt counter, not the crypto. `ValidateAndConsumeTOTP` uses a conditional UPDATE to reject a reused passcode atomically: ```go // models/auth/twofactor.go t.LastUsedPasscode = passcode n, err := db.GetEngine(ctx).ID(t.ID). Where(builder.Or(builder.IsNull{'last_used_passcode'}, builder.Neq{'last_used_passcode': passcode})). Cols('last_used_passcode').Update(t) ... return n == 1, nil ``` `totp.Validate` runs at Skew=1, so 3 of the 1,000,000 codes are valid per 30-second window. Measured observations: - 30 consecutive wrong codes all returned HTTP 200 with no lockout. - Window tolerance confirmed at offsets -1/0/+1 (3 valid codes per 30s window). - The 2FA failure branch emits no log line, so a fail2ban filter watching the log cannot see failed TOTP attempts (that log format exists only in the SSH server, `modules/ssh/ssh.go`). ## Impact An attacker with the password recovers the second factor by exhaustive guessing. With Skew=1, `p = 3 / 1,000,000 ` and expected attempts `1/p = 333,333` (the PoC hit at 309,961). The table uses a conservative 500 req/s, well under the 1,233 req/s the single-client PoC averaged: | Success chance | Attempts | Time @ 500 req/s | |---|---|---| | 50% | 231,049 | 7.7 min | | Mean (63%) | 333,333 | 11.1 min | | 90% | 767,528 | 25.6 min | | 95% | 998,578 | 33.3 min | | 99% | 1,535,057 | 51.2 min | After a hit the attacker holds a fully authenticated session and disables the victim's TOTP. ## Remediation Add an account-keyed failure counter on `twofaUid` and reject once it is exceeded: ```go func TwoFactorPost(ctx *context.Context) { uid, ok := ctx.Session.Get('twofaUid').(int64) if !ok { ctx.ServerError('UserSignIn', errors.New('not in 2FA session')); return } if failedTwoFactor(uid) >= 5 { ctx.RenderWithErrDeprecated(ctx.Tr('auth.twofa_too_many_attempts'), tplTwofa, forms.TwoFactorAuthForm{}) return } ok2, err := twofa.ValidateAndConsumeTOTP(ctx, form.Passcode) // ... on success: resetTwoFactor(uid); sign in ... incrTwoFactor(uid, 5*time.Minute) // 5 failures / 5 minutes, per account ctx.RenderWithErrDeprecated(ctx.Tr('auth.twofa_passcode_incorrect'), tplTwofa, forms.TwoFactorAuthForm{}) } ``` Keying on `twofaUid` means the ceiling cannot be widened by rotating source addresses, and five attempts per five minutes makes a 333,333-guess search infeasible. Defense in depth, independent of the counter: emit a failed-authentication log line on a wrong TOTP in the format Gitea's documented fail2ban filter already matches, so operators who rely on fail2ban gain coverage of the web 2FA path, not just SSH.

CVE-2026-123638.title: Branch protection "Protected file patterns" bypass via git C-quoted file names — push and merge gates both fail open; leads to untrusted Actions workflow execution on self-hosted runners when .gitea/** is protected
CVE-2026-123638.description: ### Summary `GetAffectedFiles` (`modules/git/diff.go`, v28.1.0 lines 303–341) is the **only** file-name source for the branch-protection *Protected file patterns* feature. It runs ```go cmd := gitcmd.NewCommand('diff', '--name-only').AddDynamicArguments(oldCommitID, newCommitID) ... path := strings.TrimSpace(scanner.Text()) // consumed raw — no -z, no C-quote unquoting affectedFiles = append(affectedFiles, path) ``` `git diff --name-only` C-quotes any path containing `'`, `\`, or a control byte, emitting e.g. `'protected/weird\'name.md'` instead of `protected/weird'name.md`. Such a line can never match a pattern like `protected/**` compiled via `glob.Compile(expr, '.', '/')` (`models/git/protected_branch.go:267`), so the protection gate fails **open**. Both enforcement paths consume this function: 1. **Direct push** — `routers/private/hook_pre_receive.go:206-208` → `pull_service.CheckFileProtection` (`services/pull/patch.go:368-381`): ```go affectedFiles, err := git.GetAffectedFiles(...) for _, affectedFile := range affectedFiles { lpath := strings.ToLower(affectedFile) for _, pat := range patterns { if pat.Match(lpath) { ... } // quoted name → no match → not protected ``` 2. **PR merge gate** — `services/pull/patch.go:439` stores `pr.ChangedProtectedFiles` → `services/pull/merge.go:718` `pb.MergeBlockedByProtectedFiles(...)` blocks the merge. Same name source, same blind spot. Meanwhile the **web UI / PR file list** goes through parsers that DO unquote (and #39781, merged 2026-10-15, frames missing unquoting as a bug): the PR view shows the file with its real name and flags it protected, while both enforcement gates let it through — a clean 'UI says protected / enforcement disagrees' divergence. ### Impact A write-access collaborator — precisely the actor this feature exists to constrain — can: 1. **Create or modify** files under any protected pattern by naming them with `'`, `\`, or a control byte. 2. **Destroy existing protected files**: rename `protected/important.yaml` to `protected/gone'x.yaml` (rename detection reports the quoted names; the old, protected-looking name disappears from the affected-file list) and then rewrite/delete its content — verified live. 3. **Execute attacker-chosen code on self-hosted runners** when the owner protects workflow paths (`.gitea/**;.github/**` — the documented pattern for this exact purpose, cf. go-gitea/gitea#33370): a workflow file pushed as `.gitea/workflows/pwn'name.yml` bypasses the gate, is still detected by the Actions workflow scanner, and a run is created and executed by the runner (full 5-hop observed chain in Appendix C; job log line: `PWNED-BY-QUOTED-NAME`). Not affected: **Unprotected file patterns** (the whitelist direction) fails CLOSED — a quoted name there makes the file *more* restricted, not less. Verified. `git fsck --strict` passes these trees; `transfer.fsckObjects` (the duplicate-tree-entry mitigation for CVE-2026-95106) does not block them — quoting is legal git output, not object corruption. ### Suggested fix Make `GetAffectedFiles` consume unquoted paths, exactly as sibling code already does: ```go cmd := gitcmd.NewCommand('diff', '--name-only', '-z').AddDynamicArguments(oldCommitID, newCommitID) // split on NUL; each entry is the raw path — no quoting, no newline ambiguity ``` (the webhook file-list and the Actions `paths:` filter already use `-z`; alternatively unquote with the same helper family that #39781 introduced for `diff-tree --raw`). A regression test should push a `protected/weird'name.md` under `protected/**` and assert rejection. ---

CVE-2026-125423.title: A repository created with auto-init accepted pushes before its in ...
CVE-2026-125423.description: A repository created with auto-init accepted pushes before its initialization had finished, and the initial commit was built in a checkout of whatever the repository already contained. A user who is allowed to create repositories could push a crafted tree during that window so that writing the README followed a symbolic link and overwrote a server-side git hook, which runs commands as the Gitea system user. The initial commit is now built in a freshly initialized directory, and a new repository only becomes ready, and accepts pushes, once its initialization is complete.

CVE-2026-125617.title: User org permissions API leaks hidden org membership and role
CVE-2026-125617.description: Any signed-in Gitea user can find out whether another user is a concealed member of a public or limited organization, and at what level, by calling `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/orgs/{org}/permissions`. The possible answers are owner, admin, write, read, or 'may create repositories'. The routes that normally answer membership questions for outsiders (`/orgs/{org}/members/{username}`, `/orgs/{org}/public_members/{username}` and `/users/{username}/orgs`) give a concealed member the same answer as a non-member. The permissions route tells them apart and adds the role. The attached reproducer runs a default build and queries as a user with no tie to the organization. It gets `is_owner: true` for the organization's concealed creator and `can_read: true` for a concealed read-team member, while the three membership routes return 404 / 404 / `[]` for both. The only access check in `GetUserOrgsPermissions` (`routers/api/v1/org/org.go`) is `HasOrgOrUserVisible` on the organization. After that, the handler returns the target's `GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel`. It never consults `org_user.is_public` or whether the caller is an org member, which is the rule `IsMember`, `ListUserOrgs` and `ListMembers` apply. Because `DEFAULT_ORG_MEMBER_VISIBLE` defaults to false, new memberships start out concealed. The caller needs an account; a token with `read:user` and `read:organization` is enough. Registration is off by default, so on a default instance this means an existing user. What leaks is membership and role only: no repository content and nothing about private organizations. Members of teams with only per-unit permissions are not revealed unless that team can create repositories. For organizations with public repositories, the assignees route already names accounts with write access. The new exposure is therefore mainly organizations without public repositories, read-only members, and exact roles. The private-organization case of this route was fixed in 57b5ed3f25 (#36798), but the per-membership check was never added. Based on a source-level reading of the history, it has been missing since the endpoint was introduced in d0a681fbc3 (#17232), first released in v1.16.0-rc1. ## Details `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/orgs/{org}/permissions` tells any signed-in user what role `{username}` holds in `{org}`, including when that membership is not public. Scanned commit: `31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7`. Attacker position: a regular user with no relation to the organization. Configuration: default. Observed on the stock build with default settings, as user `attacker`, against the public organization `victimorg` whose creator `orgowner` and team member `hiddenmember` both have `org_user.is_public = false`, and against `bystander`, who is not a member: | request (as `attacker`) | `orgowner` | `hiddenmember` | `bystander` | |---|---|---|---| | `GET /orgs/victimorg/members/{user}` | 303 → `public_members` → 404 | 303 → 404 | 303 → 404 | | `GET /orgs/victimorg/public_members/{user}` | 404 | 404 | 404 | | `GET /users/{user}/orgs` | `[]` | `[]` | `[]` | | `GET /users/{user}/orgs/victimorg/permissions` | 200, `is_owner: true` (all five fields true) | 200, `can_read: true` | 200, all five fields false | The three routes that answer 'is this user a member' give an outsider the same answer for a concealed member and a non-member. The permissions route separates them and adds the role. The handler's only visibility check is on the organization: ```go // routers/api/v1/org/org.go:157-163 if !organization.HasOrgOrUserVisible(ctx, o, ctx.Doer) { ctx.APIErrorNotFound() return } org := organization.OrgFromUser(o) authorizeLevel, err := org.GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel(ctx, ctx.ContextUser.ID) ``` `GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel` (`models/organization/org.go:416`) is `max(team.authorize)` over the target's `team_user` rows in the org. Lines 169-186 translate it into `can_read` / `can_write` / `is_admin` / `is_owner` and add `can_create_repository` from `CanCreateOrgRepo`. Neither `org_user.is_public` for the target nor the caller's own membership is consulted anywhere on the path. The route is registered at `routers/api/v1/api.go:1776-1779`. Its guards are `reqToken()`, the token scopes `read:user` and `read:organization` (a token with exactly these two scopes gets the same 200 responses), `checkTokenPublicOnly()`, and `individualPermsChecker` (`api.go:984`), which only requires that `{username}` is visible to the caller. An anonymous request gets 401. The siblings do apply the membership rule: - `IsMember` (`routers/api/v1/org/member.go:153-175`) answers directly only when the caller is an org member or a site admin; everyone else is redirected to `public_members`, and `IsPublicMember` (`member.go:204`) answers from `organization.IsPublicMembership`. - `ListUserOrgs` goes through `queryUserOrgIDs` (`models/organization/org_list.go:63-69`), which adds `is_public = true` unless the caller is the user or an admin. - `ListMembers` uses `FindOrgMembersOpts.PublicOnly()` (`models/organization/org.go:180`) to restrict non-members to public memberships. Memberships start out concealed: both `CreateOrganization` (`models/organization/org.go:350`) and `AddOrgUser` (`org.go:532`) insert the `org_user` row with `IsPublic: setting.Service.DefaultOrgMemberVisible`, and `[service] DEFAULT_ORG_MEMBER_VISIBLE` defaults to `false` (`modules/setting/service.go:244`). What the response reveals depends on `team.authorize`: - The Owners team has `authorize = owner`, so every concealed owner comes back with `is_owner: true`. - Teams with a general permission reveal their members as `can_read` / `can_write` / `is_admin`. `POST /orgs/{org}/teams` with `permission` and no `units`/`units_map` creates such a team for `read`, `write` or `admin` (`routers/api/v1/org/team.go:177-181`); the web form handler does for `write` and `admin` (`routers/web/org/teams.go:347`). Read and write teams created through the API were observed; the admin case follows from the same comparisons in the handler, and the web-form path was read from source, not run. - Teams defined per unit have `authorize = none` (`team.go:170`, `routers/web/org/teams.go:370`). A member of only such teams returns the same all-false body as a non-member, unless the team has `can_create_org_repo`, in which case `can_create_repository: true` gives the membership away. Both cases were observed on the running server. A limited organization behaves like a public one for a signed-in caller (observed: 200 with `is_owner: true`). A private organization returns 404 to non-members; that case was closed by 57b5ed3f25 (#36798), which made `HasOrgOrUserVisible` test the caller instead of the target. The per-membership check is the part that is still missing; it has been absent since the endpoint was added in `d0a681fbc3fb` ('[API] Add endpount to get user org permissions (#17232)', 2021-10-12), first released in v1.16.0-rc1. ## Impact The attacker needs an account, and what leaks is membership and role metadata only: no repository content, and nothing about private organizations. Registration is disabled by default (`DISABLE_REGISTRATION` defaults to `true`, `modules/setting/service.go:148`), so on a default instance this is an existing user; on instances with open registration it is anyone. With that, any signed-in user can test any visible username against any public or limited organization and learn whether that user is a concealed owner, or a concealed member of an admin/write/read team or of a team that may create repositories, together with that role. Iterating over usernames lists the concealed members of such an organization with their roles. This defeats the membership-visibility setting that the other organization routes enforce. That concealment is already partial elsewhere. When the organization owns a public repository, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/assignees` lists the accounts with write access to that repository to any signed-in user (observed on the same instance: it returned the concealed owner and a concealed write-team member), and issue comments label a concealed member's posts as Owner/Member (from source, not run). What the permissions route adds is organizations without public repositories, read-only members, and the exact role. ## Suggested fix The attached patch applies the rule `IsMember` already uses. In `GetUserOrgsPermissions` (`routers/api/v1/org/org.go`), right after `organization.OrgFromUser(o)` and before `GetOrgUserMaxAuthorizeLevel`, it checks who is asking. If the caller is not the target user and not a site admin, the patch checks whether the caller is a member of the organization (`org.IsOrgMember`). If not, the target's membership must be public (`organization.IsPublicMembership`), and otherwise the handler returns `ctx.APIErrorNotFound()`. A non-public membership therefore gets the same 404 as a non-membership, so the two stay indistinguishable, and this is the same 404 the other membership routes give. This changes the answer an outsider gets for a non-member from `200` with all fields false to `404`. Answers for self, site-admin and fellow-member queries are unchanged, and the existing `TestPermissionsAPI` cases, which all query as self or admin, still pass. If the 200 shape has to stay, returning the zero-valued `OrganizationPermissions` in that branch closes the leak equally. The patch also adds a regression subtest, `testHiddenMemberOfPublicOrg`, run from `TestPermissionsAPI` in `tests/integration/api_user_org_perm_test.go`. It uses the fixtures: org3 is public, user2's membership is public, user4's is not, and user5 and user8 are not members. As user8 it expects 404 for user4 and user5 and 200 with `is_owner` for user2. As user2 (a member) it expects 200 with `can_write` for user4. The test fails on the unpatched handler and passes with the patch. ## Suggested patch ```diff diff --git a/routers/api/v1/org/org.go b/routers/api/v1/org/org.go index ed450d21e9..46f5311723 100644 --- a/routers/api/v1/org/org.go +++ b/routers/api/v1/org/org.go @@ -160,6 +160,29 @@ func GetUserOrgsPermissions(ctx *context.APIContext) { } org := organization.OrgFromUser(o) + + // Like IsMember: a non-public membership is only disclosed to the user themselves, + // to site admins and to members of the organization. CVE-2026-126338.title: Code comment reply accepts foreign review ID, leaks private diff hunks
CVE-2026-126338.description:
A missing authorization check in Gitea's code-comment reply path lets any signed-in regular user read diff hunks from pull requests in private repositories they have no access to. By submitting a reply whose `reply` form field names a review from another repository, the attacker gets that review's stored diff hunk and commit SHA copied into a comment on a pull request they can comment on. The hunk is up to `[ui] CODE_COMMENT_LINES` diff lines, 4 by default, ending at the commented line. On default settings, the attached reproducer recovers a `PASSWORD=s3cr3t-of-the-victim` line from `victim/private`, while the same attacker gets 404 when asking the API for that review's comments directly. The bug is in `createCodeComment` in `services/pull/review.go`. When `reviewID != 0`, it calls `FindComments` with only `ReviewID`, `Line`, `TreePath` and `Type`, with no `IssueID` or `RepoID`. It then copies the first match's `Patch`, `CommitSHA` and `Invalidated` into the new comment. The caller, `pull_service.CreateCodeComment`, only checks that the caller's own pull request already has a code comment on that path and line. It never checks that `replyReviewID` belongs to that pull request. The attacker first comments on the matching path and line in a pull request they can comment on (they do not need a repository of their own). They then post the reply form to `POST /{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/files/reviews/comments`, and read the copied `diff_hunk` back by replying to the planted comment through the API. The leak is narrow. Each hit needs a review ID, which is sequential instance-wide but does not reveal its repository. It also needs the exact file path and line of a review comment on the new side of the diff, although the response status confirms guesses (200 for a hit, 500 for a wrong path or line, 404 for a nonexistent review). Pending reviews are affected too, but only the diff under a draft comment leaks, not the draft text. The unbound lookup was introduced in b091c994b593 ('Comments on review should have the same sha (#13448)') and first released in v1.14.0. The API reply route used here to read the hunk back exists only since v1.27.0, so on older releases the hunk is still copied but cannot be read back this way. ## Details When a code comment is posted as a reply, `createCodeComment` reuses the diff hunk stored with the first comment of the review being replied to. The review ID is the form field `reply`, and the lookup is not limited to the pull request (or repository) the request was authorized for: ```go // services/pull/review.go:218 if line > 0 { if reviewID != 0 { first, err := issues_model.FindComments(ctx, &issues_model.FindCommentsOptions{ ReviewID: reviewID, // request-controlled; no IssueID, no RepoID Line: line, TreePath: treePath, Type: issues_model.CommentTypeCode, … }) if err == nil && len(first) > 0 { commitID = first[0].CommitSHA invalidated = first[0].Invalidated patch = first[0].Patch // diff hunk of whatever repository that review belongs to } … ``` Observed at commit `31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7` with default settings: `victim/private` is a private repository whose pull request changes line 3 of `deploy/settings.env` to `PASSWORD=s3cr3t-of-the-victim`; review 1 has a comment on that line. The unrelated regular user `attacker` opens a pull request in their own `attacker/scratch`, comments on `deploy/settings.env` line 3 there, and submits the reply form with `reply=1`. The API then hands the attacker a comment in `attacker/scratch` with ``` 'diff_hunk': '@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 HOST=db.internal
 USER=app
-PASSWORD=
+PASSWORD=s3cr3t-of-the-victim' ``` and the `commit_id` of the victim's commit, while `GET /api/v1/repos/victim/private/pulls/1/reviews/1/comments` answers the attacker 404. The path from the request to the copy: 1. `POST /{username}/{reponame}/pulls/{index}/files/reviews/comments` (`routers/web/web.go:1662`) sits behind `context.RepoMustNotBeArchived()` (`:1664`) and `optSignIn, context.RepoAssignment, repo.MustAllowPulls, reqUnitPullsReader` (`:1667`). All of them look at the repository in the URL, which can be the attacker's own. 2. `repo.CreateCodeComment` (`routers/web/repo/pull_review.go:64`) loads the pull request from the URL with `GetActionIssue` and passes `form.Reply` (`services/forms/repo_form.go:471`) unchecked as `replyReviewID` (`:98`). In the UI the field is filled by `templates/repo/diff/comment_form.tmpl:34` with the review ID of the conversation being replied to. 3. `pull_service.CreateCodeComment` (`services/pull/review.go:119-125`) asks only `ReviewExists(ctx, issue, treePath, line)` (`models/issues/review.go:451`): does the *caller's* pull request already have a code comment on that path and line? The attacker creates that comment first; the path does not have to exist in their pull request. `replyReviewID` is never compared with `issue.ID`. 4. `createCodeComment(…, replyReviewID, …)` runs the lookup quoted above. `FindCommentsOptions.ToConds` (`models/issues/comment.go:1094-1119`) adds a repository or issue condition only when `RepoID` / `IssueID` are set, so the query is `review_id = ? AND line = ? AND tree_path = ? AND type = code` over all repositories. The new comment is then created on the caller's pull request with `CommitSHA: commitID`, `ReviewID: reviewID`, `Patch: patch` (`services/pull/review.go:287-300`). 5. Reading it back: the form's HTML response renders the conversation with the hunk of its first comment (the attacker's own). The stored hunk is exposed as `diff_hunk` / `commit_id` by `convert.ToPullReviewComment` (`services/convert/pull_review.go:113-115`). `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/comments/{id}/replies` (`CreatePullReviewCommentReply`, `routers/api/v1/repo/pull_review.go:209`) returns that JSON for the reply it creates. This route cannot name a foreign review by itself, because it loads the parent comment with `GetCommentWithRepoID(ctx, ctx.Repo.Repository.ID, …)` and takes `parent.ReviewID`; but the comment planted in step 4 is in the attacker's repository and carries the foreign `ReviewID`, so a reply to it goes through the same unbound lookup and returns the victim's hunk. The unbound lookup was introduced in `b091c994b593` ('Comments on review should have the same sha (#13448)', 2020-11-09) and first released in v1.14.0. The API reply route used in step 5 to read the hunk back only exists since v1.27.0 (`331450b17a`, 2026-04-27), so on older releases the hunk is still copied into the attacker's comment but this way of reading it back is not available. The notification mail template (`templates/mail/repo/issue/default.tmpl:56`) also prints the stored hunk; that channel was not tested (no mail offline). Other users of a request-supplied review ID bind it: `DismissReview` compares `review.Issue.RepoID` with the repository (`services/pull/review.go:420-423`), and the API's `prepareSingleReview` rejects `review.IssueID != pr.IssueID` and pending reviews of other users (`routers/api/v1/repo/pull_review.go:722-732`). ## Impact A signed-in regular user on a default configuration reads diff hunks of pull requests in repositories they have no access to, within narrow limits: each hit yields at most the last `[ui] CODE_COMMENT_LINES` (default 4) diff lines ending at a line that carries a review comment, plus the commit SHA; only comments on the new side of the diff are reachable (the lookup runs for `line > 0`); and for each hunk the attacker must supply the review ID, the exact file path and the line. They need one pull request they can comment on. No repository of their own is needed: a third account with no repository got the same result (HTTP 200) on somebody else's public pull request, once a code comment existed on that path and line there. Review IDs are one auto-increment sequence for the whole instance, so the attacker's own reviews reveal the current range, but an ID does not tell which repository its review belongs to, so the leak cannot be aimed at one chosen repository. Path and line have to be known (former collaborator, private fork of a public project, conventional file names) or guessed; each guess costs two requests (the comment on that path and line in the attacker's pull request, then the reply) and the reply's status confirms it. Observed: 200 for a hit, 500 for a wrong path or line on an existing foreign review (`git blame` is run on that review's commit ID in the attacker's repository and fails with `bad object`), 404 for a review ID that does not exist; the two misses create no comment. The copy also happens for a review that is still pending: a reply naming the victim's unsubmitted review stored the diff hunk under its draft comment in the attacker's comment, and an API reply to that comment returned it. What leaks is the diff under the draft, not the draft comment's text. In that case the planted comment is not rendered in the form's response, so its ID has to be derived from the sequential comment IDs; this step was checked with the ID taken from the database and is not part of the reproducer. As a side effect the attacker's comment row points to a review of another repository (`comment.review_id`). ## Suggested fix The attached patch checks the caller-supplied review ID in `pull_service.CreateCodeComment`, the one service function both the web reply form and the API reply endpoint go through. It loads the review and rejects it with `ErrReviewNotExist` unless it is a review of the pull request being commented on and, if still pending, belongs to the doer (as `prepareSingleReview` does), and it additionally binds the lookup in `createCodeComment` to the issue: ```diff --- a/services/pull/review.go +++ b/services/pull/review.go @@ -117,6 +117,15 @@ func CreateCodeComment( if !pendingReview && replyReviewID != 0 { + // The review ID is provided by the caller, make sure it is a review of this pull request which the doer can see + replyReview, err := issues_model.GetReviewByID(ctx, replyReviewID) + if err != nil { + return nil, err + } + if replyReview.IssueID != issue.ID || (replyReview.Type == issues_model.ReviewTypePending && replyReview.ReviewerID != doer.ID) { + return nil, issues_model.ErrReviewNotExist{ID: replyReviewID} + } + // It's not part of a review; maybe a reply to a review comment or a single comment. @@ -218,6 +227,7 @@ func createCodeComment( first, err := issues_model.FindComments(ctx, &issues_model.FindCommentsOptions{ + IssueID: issue.ID, ReviewID: reviewID, ``` The web handler needs no change: `ctx.ServerError` already answers 404 for errors wrapping `util.ErrNotExist` (`services/context/context_response.go:170`). In `CreatePullReviewCommentReply` the patch routes the error through `ctx.APIErrorAuto(err)` instead of `ctx.APIErrorInternal(err)`, so a rejected review yields 404 instead of 500. A reply naming a nonexistent or foreign review is refused and no comment is created; replies to a review of the same pull request are unaffected. Unlike `prepareSingleReview`, there is no exception for site admins on other users' pending reviews. The patch adds a regression test, `TestCreateCodeCommentReplyReview` in `services/pull/review_test.go`, that calls `pull_service.CreateCodeComment` with the ID of a review created on a pull request of another repository (fixtures: issue 3 as the caller's, issue 12 as the foreign one), with another user's pending review of the same pull request, and with a non-existent ID, each expecting `IsErrReviewNotExist` and no comment created; a reply to a review of the same pull request still succeeds and inherits its patch. With the patch applied the reproducer prints `OK`. Comment rows already planted on a live instance keep the copied hunk; code comments whose `review_id` belongs to a review of a different issue identify past abuse. ## Suggested patch ```diff diff err != nil { diff --git a/services/pull/review.go b/services/pull/review.go index 3d42330637..07faf42120 100644 --- a/services/pull/review.go +++ b/services/pull/review.go @@ -117,6 +117,15 @@ func replyReview.IssueID != issue.ID || (replyReview.Type == issues_model.ReviewTypePending && replyReview.ReviewerID != doer.ID) { + return nil, issues_model.ErrReviewNotExist{ID: replyReviewID} + } + // CVE-2026-128365.title: RemoveTeamReviewRequest treats team id 2 as Actions user, bypassing approvals
CVE-2026-128365.description: A user with write access to an organization repository can merge their own pull request into a branch protected by 'required approvals' without any human review. They approve the PR with an Actions job token, then request and withdraw a review from the team whose id is 2, which turns the `gitea-actions` approval into an official one. This only affects the one organization on the instance that owns team id 2, and only when that team counts as an official reviewer for the branch (write access to code, or listed in the approvals whitelist). The attacker does not need to be a member of that team. The bug is in `RemoveTeamReviewRequest` (`models/issues/review.go`, around lines 895–912). When a team review request is withdrawn, it looks up 'the latest review of the team' with `GetReviewByIssueIDAndUserID(ctx, issue.ID, -reviewer.ID)` and sets `official=true` on whatever row it finds. No review is ever stored under a negated team id. Negative reviewer ids are system users, though, and `ActionsUserID = -2` is the identity behind every Actions job token. Any job token, including one from a runner the attacker registers on their own repository, can read a public repository and post a review. That review is normally stored as `official=false` and does not count toward required approvals. Once the team 2 request is withdrawn, `GetGrantedApprovalsCount` counts it and the merge goes through. The gain is limited to one approval per pull request, and the PR visibly shows `gitea-actions` as its reviewer. The attached reproducer runs a default sqlite instance. The merge is refused with `405 Does not have enough approvals`, still refused after withdrawing an otherwise identical team with id 3, and accepted with `200` after withdrawing team id 2. A user with no access to the organization can flip the flag the same way from a fork PR, but cannot merge it themselves. The lookup dates from v1.13.0 and was harmless until the Actions user (id -2) arrived in 4011821c946e, first released in v1.19.0. ## Details Scanned commit `31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7`, default configuration. Attacker: a regular user with write access to an organization repository whose protected branch requires approvals. Entry point: `DELETE /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/requested_reviewers` (or the web form `POST /{owner}/{repo}/issues/request_review`). When a team review request is withdrawn, `RemoveTeamReviewRequest` tries to restore 'the latest official review from that team' and looks it up under the reviewer id `-team.ID`: ```go // models/issues/review.go:895 official, err := IsOfficialReviewerTeam(ctx, issue, reviewer) … if official { // recalculate which is the latest official review from that team review, err := GetReviewByIssueIDAndUserID(ctx, issue.ID, -reviewer.ID) … if review != nil { if _, err := db.Exec(ctx, 'UPDATE `review` SET official=? WHERE id=?', true, review.ID); err != nil { ``` No review is ever stored with `reviewer_id = -teamID`: a team request is a row with `reviewer_team_id` set (`AddTeamReviewRequest`, `models/issues/review.go:848`), and reviews by team members carry the member's own id. Negative `reviewer_id` values do exist, though. They are the system users of `models/user/user_system.go:49-54`, and `ActionsUserID = -2` is the doer behind every Actions job token. For the team with id 2 the lookup therefore returns the latest approve/reject/request review of `gitea-actions` on that pull request, and the `UPDATE` marks it official. The condition checked before it (`IsOfficialReviewerTeam`) is about the team, not about the author of the row being updated. On a running instance: a pull request approved only by a job token is refused with `405 Does not have enough approvals`; after its author requests and withdraws a review from the team with id 2, the same merge returns `200`. ### The path `mallory` is a member of a team with write access in the organization `acme`. `acme/app` is public and its `main` branch has a protection rule with `required_approvals: 1`. The team `developers` has id 2. 1. `mallory` opens pull request #1 from a branch of `acme/app`. 2. `mallory` obtains an Actions job token. All job tokens act as user -2, so any one will do; the simplest source is a repository of `mallory`'s own with a runner registered for it (`POST /api/v1/repos/mallory/mine/actions/runners/registration-token`). A job token gets read access to other public repositories (`GetActionsUserRepoPermission`, `models/perm/access/repo_permission.go:337-367`). 3. With the job token `mallory` sends `POST /api/v1/repos/acme/app/pulls/1/reviews {'event':'APPROVED'}`. The route needs `reqToken()` and read access to code (`routers/api/v1/api.go:1515-1517`, group guards at `:1535`). `SubmitReview` decides the `official` flag with `IsOfficialReviewer` (`models/issues/review.go:494`), which ends in `IsUserOfficialReviewer` → `HasAccessUnit(…, unit.TypeCode, AccessModeWrite)` (`models/git/protected_branch.go:264-276`). That helper evaluates user -2 as a plain user without write access, so the review is stored with `official=false` and the merge is refused. Up to here everything works as intended. 4. `mallory` sends `POST` and then `DELETE /api/v1/repos/acme/app/pulls/1/requested_reviewers {'team_reviewers':['developers']}`. Both go through `apiReviewRequest` (`routers/api/v1/repo/pull_review.go:867`) to `issue_service.TeamReviewRequest` (`services/issue/review_request.go:180`). Its only check, `isValidTeamReviewRequest`, accepts the poster of the pull request (`CanDoerChangeReviewRequests`, `services/issue/review_request.go:240`). The `DELETE` reaches the code quoted above. `IsOfficialReviewerTeam` (`models/issues/review.go:308`) is true because the team has write access to code (with an approvals whitelist enabled it is true when the team is on the whitelist). The lookup with `-2` finds the bot's approval and sets `official=true`. 5. `GetGrantedApprovalsCount` (`models/issues/pull.go:770`) counts rows with `type=approve AND official=true`, now finds one, and `POST /api/v1/repos/acme/app/pulls/1/merge` succeeds. Doing step 4 with a second team that has the same permissions and members but id 3 leaves the review at `official=false` and the merge refused, which isolates the id collision as the cause. The web handler `UpdatePullReviewRequest` (`routers/web/repo/pull_review.go:385-399`, form fields `id=-2&action=detach`) calls the same `TeamReviewRequest`; that route was read, not exercised. The block dates from team review requests (`8be3e439c2b3`, 'Add team support for review request (#12039)', 2020-10-13), when no review could carry a negative reviewer id. It became harmful with the Actions user id -2, introduced in `4011821c946e` ('Implement actions (#21937)', 2023-01-31), first released in v1.19.0 (Actions became enabled by default in v1.21.0). This is from reading the history; older trees could not be built to bisect. ## Impact A user with write access who is subject to 'required approvals' merges their own change into the protected branch with no reviewer involved. The pull request shows a single approval, by `gitea-actions`. The precondition that limits this is the id: the team must have id 2, the only negated team id that is a system user able to submit reviews. Team ids are instance-wide and sequential, so this is the second team ever created on the instance, and exactly one organization owns it. On an instance with a single organization that is usually the first team created after `Owners`; if a second organization was created before any custom team, it is that organization's `Owners` team. The team has to count as an official reviewer team for the branch (write access to code, or listed in the approvals whitelist); the attacker does not need to be a member of it. Organizations that do not own team 2 are not affected. Both points were checked in a separate run: with `acme/Owners` as team 2 (another organization created before `acme`) and `mallory` a plain write collaborator with no custom team, the approval becomes official and the merge returns `200`; with the approvals whitelist enabled and team 2 not listed, the flag stays false and the merge is refused. The gain is one approval per pull request. By source, a further approval with a job token first clears `official` on all earlier reviews of user -2 (`models/issues/review.go:491`) and is itself stored as not official, and the lookup in `RemoveTeamReviewRequest` returns only the latest row (`:585-593`), so at most one `gitea-actions` review is official at a time. Rules with `required_approvals` of 2 or more still need genuine reviewers for the rest. This was not part of the reproducer. The flag is also reachable without any access to the organization: a user who opens a pull request from a fork against a public repository of that organization can perform steps 2-4 (the poster may request and withdraw team reviews), and the approval becomes official. This was observed in a separate run; that user's own merge attempt is refused with `405 User not allowed to merge PR`, so it still takes somebody with merge rights to merge a pull request that now displays its approval requirement as met. Not exercised: private repositories. There the job token must come from a job that can read the target repository (a workflow in that repository or one allowed by the owner's cross-repository Actions settings) instead of from an unrelated repository of the attacker. ## Suggested fix The attached patch removes the block from `RemoveTeamReviewRequest` (`models/issues/review.go:895-912`). It cannot find what its comment describes: team requests never change the `official` flag of a member's review (`AddTeamReviewRequest` clears it only on rows with `reviewer_team_id = team`, `models/issues/review.go:855`), so there is nothing to restore when the request is withdrawn. The rest of `RemoveTeamReviewRequest` (deleting the request row, creating the comment) and the user-level counterpart `RemoveReviewRequest` are unchanged. ```diff --- a/models/issues/review.go +++ b/models/issues/review.go @@ -892,25 +892,6 @@ func RemoveTeamReviewRequest(ctx context.Context, issue *Issue, reviewer *organi return nil, err } - official, err := IsOfficialReviewerTeam(ctx, issue, reviewer) - if err != nil { - return nil, fmt.Errorf('isOfficialReviewerTeam(): %w', err) - } - - if official { - // recalculate which is the latest official review from that team - review, err := GetReviewByIssueIDAndUserID(ctx, issue.ID, -reviewer.ID) - if err != nil && !IsErrReviewNotExist(err) { - return nil, err - } - - if review != nil { - if _, err := db.Exec(ctx, 'UPDATE `review` SET official=? WHERE id=?', true, review.ID); err != nil { - return nil, err - } - } - } - if doer == nil { return nil, nil } ``` With the attached patch applied to a clean checkout and the server rebuilt, the reproducer prints `OK`. The patch also adds a regression test to `models/issues/review_test.go` (with the import `gitea.dev/models/organization`); it fails on the scanned commit at the last assertion and passes with the change. In the fixtures, team 2 is `org3/team1` and issue 12 is a pull request of `org3/repo3`: ```go func TestRemoveTeamReviewRequestDoesNotTouchSystemUserReview(t *testing.T) { assert.NoError(t, unittest.PrepareTestDatabase()) issue := unittest.AssertExistsAndLoadBean(t, &issues_model.Issue{ID: 12}) assert.NoError(t, issue.LoadRepo(t.Context())) team := unittest.AssertExistsAndLoadBean(t, &organization.Team{ID: -user_model.ActionsUserID}) doer := unittest.AssertExistsAndLoadBean(t, &user_model.User{ID: 2}) assert.NoError(t, db.Insert(t.Context(), &git_model.ProtectedBranch{RepoID: issue.RepoID, RuleName: 'master', RequiredApprovals: 1})) review, err := issues_model.CreateReview(t.Context(), issues_model.CreateReviewOptions{ Type: issues_model.ReviewTypeApprove, Issue: issue, Reviewer: user_model.NewActionsUser(), Official: false, }) assert.NoError(t, err) _, err = issues_model.AddTeamReviewRequest(t.Context(), issue, team, doer, false) assert.NoError(t, err) _, err = issues_model.RemoveTeamReviewRequest(t.Context(), issue, team, doer) assert.NoError(t, err) review = unittest.AssertExistsAndLoadBean(t, &issues_model.Review{ID: review.ID}) assert.False(t, review.Official) } ``` The patch does not repair rows that were already flipped: on an instance that was hit, reviews with `reviewer_id < 0` and `official = true` stay official, which may be worth a release note. ## Suggested patch ```diff diff --git a/models/issues/review.go b/models/issues/review.go index bb1541df2e..1c4f76385e 100644 --- a/models/issues/review.go +++ b/models/issues/review.go @@ -892,25 +892,6 @@ func RemoveTeamReviewRequest(ctx context.Context, issue *Issue, reviewer *organi return nil, err } - CVE-2026-129337.title: Read-only users can push over HTTP to repositories being migrated
CVE-2026-129337.description: A user with only read access to a repository can push to it over HTTP while it is being imported. The pushed commits create or overwrite its branches and tags, become part of the imported repository, and leave no entry in its activity feed. For a public repository this is any registered user; for a private one it is anyone with read access, such as a read-only team member. The attached reproducer has an unrelated read-only user overwrite `main` of another user's repository during a migration, and shows the identical push being refused with 'User permission denied for writing' once the import has finished. The cause is in `httpBase` (`routers/web/repo/githttp.go`). Since the AGit support added in 370516883717 (#14295, first released in v1.16.0-rc1), it lowers the required mode for `git-receive-pack` on an existing code repository to read and leaves the write check to the `pre-receive` hook. Unlike the SSH path (`routers/private/serv.go`) and the web routes, it never refuses a repository whose status is `RepositoryBeingMigrated`. Meanwhile, `MigrateRepositoryGitData` (`services/repository/migrate.go`) places a plain `git clone --mirror` with no Gitea hooks at the served location. The delegate hooks are only written by `CleanUpMigrateInfo` after the clone, wiki clone, branch sync and LFS download, so during that time `git receive-pack` runs with no write check at all. The attacker has to push inside this window, but does not need a slow or cooperating import source. Against a one-commit import that finished in 0.12 s, a blind push loop landed a branch in 4 of 5 runs. If the import fails before the hooks are installed (for example a wiki clone or LFS download error), the repository stays in the being-migrated state without hooks, and readers can keep pushing until the owner deletes or retries it. Imports created as pull mirrors are not affected. The bug grants write access only: nothing becomes readable that was not already, and no code runs on the server. ## Details Scanned commit `31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7`. Attacker: a regular user who can read the repository (any registered user for a public one, a read-only team member for a private one). Configuration: default. Entry point: `git push` over HTTP, i.e. `POST /{owner}/{repo}.git/git-receive-pack`. Two things combine. First, git over HTTP does not check write permission for a push to an existing code repository. It lowers the required mode to read (so that readers can push AGit `refs/for/*`) and leaves the decision to the `pre-receive` hook (`routers/web/repo/githttp.go:184-204`): ```go if repoExist { // Only the main code repo accepts refs/for pushes, so wiki pushes must keep write checks. if !isWiki { accessMode = perm.AccessModeRead } … if !p.CanAccess(accessMode, unitType) { ctx.PlainText(http.StatusNotFound, 'Repository not found') return nil } if !isPull && repo.IsMirror { ``` `httpBase` never looks at `repo.Status`. The SSH path does (`routers/private/serv.go:161`), and so do the web routes (`services/context/repo.go:711`): ```go if repo.IsBeingCreated() { ctx.PrivateUserErrorf(http.StatusForbidden, 'Repository is being created, you could retry after it finished') return } ``` The lowering to read was introduced in `370516883717` ('Add agit flow support in gitea (#14295)', 2021-07-28), first released in v1.16.0-rc1; before it, `httpBase` refused the same push with 403 before git ran. Second, a repository that is being migrated has no Gitea hooks for most of the import. The database row already exists with `Status: RepositoryBeingMigrated` (`routers/api/v1/repo/migrate.go:179`, `services/task/task.go:117`), so the repository resolves on the git routes and the usual read permission applies. `MigrateRepositoryGitData` then replaces its directory with a plain clone at the final, served location (`services/repository/migrate.go:88-102`): ```go if err := git.DeleteRepository(ctx, repo); err != nil { … } if err := git.CloneExternalRepo(ctx, opts.CloneAddr, repo, git.CloneRepoOptions{ Mirror: true, … ``` `CloneExternalRepo` (`modules/git/clone.go:13`) is `git clone --mirror -- <url> <RepoLocalPath(repo)>`; what it creates contains git's `*.sample` hooks only. The delegate hooks are written by `CleanUpMigrateInfo` → `git.CreateDelegateHooks` (`migrate.go:240`, `:264`), the last step of the function. Between the two lie the clone itself, `WriteCommitGraph` (`:104`), the wiki probe and wiki clone (`:109`), the branch and tag sync (`:147-157`) and the download of all LFS objects (`:165`). If the import fails in between (wiki clone error, LFS download error, clone timeout), the repository is left with status `RepositoryBeingMigrated` and without hooks, and readers can still push to it after the failed import. So mallory's request passes `httpBase` with read permission, `git receive-pack` runs in a directory without `pre-receive`, and git updates the ref. The write check (`routers/private/hook_pre_receive.go:60`) never runs. `post-receive` is missing as well: after mallory's push the repository's activity feed stayed empty, while a later push by alice added a `commit_repo` entry. `SyncRepoBranchesWithRepo` (`migrate.go:147`) then records whatever the refs point to as the imported state. The window opens as soon as `git clone` has initialised the directory, before any object has arrived. With the remote holding back its pack, mallory's push of a new root commit to `refs/heads/evil` was accepted and the finished import had the branches `evil` and `main`. A push to `refs/heads/main` in that phase is accepted as well, but Gitea's own `git clone --mirror` then aborts (`initial ref transaction called with existing refs`, git 2.47.3) and the import fails with 422, which leaves the repository in the hookless state described above. Overwriting `main` works once the clone has written its refs, which is what the reproducer does. Imports created as pull mirrors are not affected: their row has `IsMirror` set from the start and `githttp.go:201` answers the same push with `mirror repository is read-only`. ## Impact A user with read access to a repository can write to any of its branches and tags while it is being imported (default settings, stock `git` client, the user's own password), and the result looks like imported history: the push leaves no entry in the activity feed. For a public repository that is every registered user; for a private one it is anyone who has read access from the moment the repository is created. That case was checked as well: a member of an organization team with read permission on all repositories pushed to `main` and created a tag in a private repository of that organization while an owner imported it. The precondition is timing. The victim must be running an import, and the attacker must push before its git phase ends, which lasts as long as the clone, the wiki clone and the LFS download take. The repository answers API and git requests of its readers during that time, so the start of an import can be watched for. No slow or cooperating import source is needed: against a one-commit import that finished in 0.12 s, a blind loop of pushes landed a branch in 4 of 5 runs. The window does not always close either: an import that fails between the clone and the hook installation leaves a repository that readers can keep pushing to until the owner deletes or retries it, and a push to `main` during the clone is one way to make the import fail. Once an import has finished, the same user cannot push. Nothing becomes readable that was not before, and no code runs on the server. _Reported by the Anthropic OSS scanner, finding ANT-2026-2TN6AY02 (scan gitea-20261022-004), commit 31626de2a6cdd3e1fe93216e4ac80f511297f1e7._

CVE-2026-129525.title: Issues-only members can read pull request data through /issues/{index}
CVE-2026-129525.description: ## Affected versions Reproduced on Gitea `v1.27.1` and on `main` at commit `298d73cde6bcb36de6cc24dc436074fb0c8b1a39`. ## Test setup Official `gitea/gitea:1.27.1` Linux container with SQLite. `INSTALL_LOCK`, the database path, and a loopback `ROOT_URL` were set only to automate installation. No security-relevant default was changed. ## Summary Several `/issues/{index}` API handlers load an issue or pull request from Gitea's shared index namespace without checking which repository unit it belongs to. In a private repository, a member with Issues access but no Pull Requests access can therefore read pull request data. The clearest example is the timeline endpoint: for the same token and pull request, `GET /issues/{index}/timeline` returns comment bodies while the guarded sibling `GET /issues/{index}/comments` returns 404. ## Root cause The `/issues` route group is guarded by `mustEnableIssuesOrPulls` (`routers/api/v1/api.go:769` and `:1568-1668`), which allows callers who can read either unit. After resolving `{index}`, these handlers do not call `CanReadIssuesOrPulls(issue.IsPull)`: - `ListIssueCommentsAndTimeline` — `routers/api/v1/repo/issue_comment.go:123` - `GetIssueAttachment` and `ListIssueAttachments` — `routers/api/v1/repo/issue_attachment.go:25` and `:74` - `ListIssueLabels` — `routers/api/v1/repo/issue_label.go:21` - `setIssueSubscription`, `CheckIssueSubscription`, and `GetIssueSubscribers` — `routers/api/v1/repo/issue_subscription.go:106`, `:157`, and `:215` The adjacent `ListIssueComments` handler performs the missing check at `routers/api/v1/repo/issue_comment.go:76`. ## Impact An Issues-only member can read pull request comment bodies. The other confirmed effects are limited to attachment metadata, label associations, subscriber identities, subscription state, and setting or clearing watch state. Attachment contents, the pull request body, and inline review comments were not exposed. Content-writing endpoints remained denied. The attacker must already be an authenticated repository member with access through another unit. ## Suggested fix After resolving `{index}`, call `CanReadIssuesOrPulls(issue.IsPull)` in each handler. A shared authorized loader for issue and pull request indices would make the check harder to omit. ## Relationship to prior advisories CVE-2026-27783 (GHSA-3fwp-p5rj-2pxf, fixed in `v1.26.2`) covered missing repository-unit route guards on the issue-template API. This report affects different handlers: the route admits Issues-or-Pull Requests users, but the resolved object's unit is never checked. ## AI-tool disclosure I used an LLM to help identify candidate authorization gaps. I reproduced the behavior manually against local Gitea instances and checked the report against the source at the tested commit. --- ## Also covers (added by the Gitea maintainers) The same missing `CanReadIssuesOrPulls(issue.IsPull)` check was reported in later advisories, which were closed as duplicates of this one. The fix must cover these too: - `POST` / `DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{index}/reactions` (`changeIssueReaction`): a user who can read only one of the Issues / Pull Requests units can add or remove reactions on an object of the other unit. - `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{index}/times` (`ListTrackedTimes`): returns the tracked times of a pull request to an Issues-only user. - Web route `GET /{owner}/{repo}/issues/search?type=pulls`: returns pull request titles and bodies to an Issues-only member. The `type` / `isPull` filter has to be limited to the units the user can read, as the API's `ListIssues` already does. This route is not under the API `/issues/{index}` group, so it needs its own fix. - The reverse direction: a user who can read only Pull Requests can act on issues through the same handlers.

CVE-2026-60018.title: Gitea's OneDev migration downloader reads the entire remote versi ...
CVE-2026-60018.description: Gitea's OneDev migration downloader reads the entire remote version response into memory without a size limit and uses a client without a timeout. CVE-2026-60021.description: Gitea's initial GitLab migration version probe uses an HTTP client without a timeout and does not attach the migration task's cancellation context. The request continues after task cancellation and can exhaust the migration worker pool, preventing other migrations from progressing.

CVE-2026-62925.title: Gitea parses Alpine package uploads before enforcing package-size ...
CVE-2026-62925.description: Gitea parses Alpine package uploads before enforcing package-size quotas and does not bound the decompressed .PKGINFO data or its dependency and provides entry counts. On memory-constrained deployments, this can terminate the process or otherwise disrupt availability.

CVE-2026-63021.description: Gitea's Swift package parser limits each manifest to 128 KiB but does not limit the number of manifests or their aggregate size before reading them into memory. An authenticated user with package-publish permission can upload a highly compressed archive containing many manifests, causing allocations far larger than the uploaded archive. This can exhaust memory, terminate the process, or cause request failures.

CVE-2026-63792.description: Gitea's collaborative-owner authorization path for reading cross-repository reusable workflows does not exclude fork pull request runs. CVE-2026-66849.description: Gitea's package registry grants authenticated users read access to packages owned by Limited-visibility users without excluding restricted accounts. The issue affects user-owned package registries and exposes package contents across the intended authorization boundary.

CVE-2026-66853.description: Gitea's user organization-list API includes Limited-visibility organizations for authenticated restricted accounts without applying the visibility restriction enforced by the single-organization endpoint. A restricted user can list a known user's public organization memberships and retrieve limited organizations' names, descriptions, and avatars. This exposes organization metadata that should be hidden from the requesting account.

CVE-2026-66874.title: For pull request events, Gitea reads workflow definitions from th ...
CVE-2026-66874.description: For pull request events, Gitea reads workflow definitions from the pull request head and posts a synthetic skipped status when workflow branch or path filters exclude execution. A fork pull request author can supply a workflow matching a required status context but deliberately prevent it from running. Because skipped statuses count as success, branch protection or organization-required workflow checks can appear satisfied without the mandated workflow executing; no runner or maintainer approval is required for this path.

CVE-2026-66877.title: Gitea enforces first-time fork contributor approval by blocking j ...
CVE-2026-66877.description: Gitea enforces first-time fork contributor approval by blocking jobs, but some job transition and dispatch paths do not re-check the run's approval requirement. A separate run sharing a job-level concurrency group can cancel a pending job and cause its blocked sibling jobs to be re-emitted and dispatched without approval. This allows unreviewed workflow code to execute on self-hosted runners; fork secrets remain withheld and the run token remains read-only.

CVE-2026-67577.description: Gitea's activity-feed and contribution-heatmap API handlers do not apply the profile visibility check for restricted accounts viewing Limited-visibility users. A restricted user can retrieve activity records and contribution timestamps that the corresponding profile routes deny. Exposed activity can include repository names, commit messages, and issue or pull request events associated with qualifying public-repository activity.

CVE-2026-68957.title: Gitea's API and web issue-search paths do not treat restricted ac ...

A restricted user can search and retrieve issue titles and bodies that should be hidden by the owner's visibility policy. Keyword matching can also reveal that hidden issue content or comments contain a supplied term.
